    <title>A former Siemens CEO thought he was investing $2.5 million in Deepak Chopra’s  app. Prosecutors say it was fraud.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T15:16:25Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/klaus-kleinfeld-deepak-chopra-app-wanja-oberhof-healing-company-fraud-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aafefe34a3706ac06f853f2?format=jpeg" height="2400" width="3600" alt="Klaus Kleinfeld"><figcaption>Federal prosecutors say Klaus Kleinfeld was defrauded of nearly $2 million.<p class="copyright">Brendan Smialowski/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Prosecutors say a startup co-founder bilked former Siemens CEO Klaus Kleinfeld of nearly $2 million.</li><li>Kleinfeld thought he was investing in Deepak Chopra's wellness and meditation app.</li><li>Chopra's company, Chopra Global, no longer has any relationship with the startup, his lawyer said.</li></ul><p>In 2023, a wellness entrepreneur pitched Klaus Kleinfeld, the former CEO of Siemens and Alcoa, on an opportunity to invest in <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/deepak-chopra-first-psychedelic-trip-lsd-mother-teresa-poster-2021-6">Deepak Chopra's</a> meditation app.</p><p>Kleinfeld invested $2.5 million. Now federal prosecutors say the entrepreneur, Wanja Oberhof, embezzled most of that money, using it for personal expenses including back rent on his nearly $20,000-per-month Manhattan penthouse.</p><p>In the criminal complaint against Oberhof filed in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, the investor is identified as "Victim-1." A spokesperson for Kleinfeld confirmed that he was the investor.</p><p>Oberhof co-founded the Healing Company with his wife, Anabel Oelmann, a former model and owner of a CBD oil company, with the aim of acquiring a stable of wellness brands. Chopra, the <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/deepak-chopra-how-to-be-mindful-2015-12">author, physician, and wellness guru</a>, became the Healing Company's chief scientific advisor in 2022. The startup in March 2023 struck a deal with Chopra's company, Chopra Global, to acquire Chopra's consumer product line, including a detox kit and body oils; the Chopra meditation and wellbeing app; and licensed Chopra health retreats at resorts and spas, corporate filings show.</p><p>Chopra Global terminated its deal with the Healing Company in July 2024, and no longer has any relationship with the Healing Company or its affiliates, an attorney for Chopra and his company told Business Insider.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aaff1436794a2984cfcaee1?format=jpeg" height="3334" width="5000" alt="Deepak Chopra"><figcaption>Deepak Chopra&#39;s company ended its deal with the Healing Company in 2024.<p class="copyright">Dave Benett/Getty Images for Compassionate Films</p></figcaption></figure><p>According to the criminal complaint, the Healing Company borrowed about $1.6 million against its line of credit for a March 2023 deal with an author and alternative medicine advocate. The details of the transaction match details of the Chopra deal disclosed in the Healing Company's corporate filings.</p><p>The following account is based on the criminal complaint:</p><p>Oberhof and <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/alcoa-earnings-q3-2016-2016-10">Kleinfeld</a>, both Germans, had met in Germany through a mutual friend. When they reconnected in New York in 2023, Kleinfeld was interested in the startup's newly acquired meditation app. Early the following year, the Healing Company defaulted on its credit line. Oberhof and Kleinfeld discussed moving the author's app and other assets to a new entity, in which Kleinfeld would invest. Kleinfeld understood from Oberhof that Oberhof could only move the assets if Oberhof paid back the loan against the line of credit. They agreed that $1 million of Kleinfeld's $2.5 million investment would be used to pay back the lender.</p><p>Instead of paying back the lender, Oberhof took most of the money for himself, moving more than $1.8 million of it to a German bank account, according to the complaint.</p><p>An attorney for Oberhof declined to comment.</p><p>Sources close to Kleinfeld say that his lawyers approached US authorities with evidence of the alleged fraud a few weeks ago. Officials were already building a case, the sources said.</p><p>Oberhof was charged with one count of wire fraud and made an initial appearance in Manhattan federal court on Monday. He hasn't yet entered a plea. Oberhof is being held at Metropolitan Detention Center, the federal jail in Brooklyn that also houses Venezuela's former president Nicolás Maduro.</p><p><em>Herbert Bauernebel contributed reporting.</em></p><p><em>The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, The Telegraph, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/klaus-kleinfeld-deepak-chopra-app-wanja-oberhof-healing-company-fraud-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T15:16:25Z</published>

    <title>I make this 6-ingredient slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip every game day. It's always a crowd-pleaser.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T13:12:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/easy-recipe-slow-cooker-buffalo-chicken-dip-game-day</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad70d76794a2984cfca874?format=jpeg" height="1834" width="2751" alt="tortilla chip dipped in buffalo chicken dip"><figcaption>The Buffalo chicken dip requires only six ingredients.<p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>I make the same Buffalo chicken dip for every party, game day, and Super Bowl.</li><li>It takes only six ingredients, plus seasonings, and comes together in a slow cooker.</li><li>It's a crowd-pleaser and unbelievably easy to make.</li></ul><p>Football Sundays are officially back, and my recipe for easy <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/football-game-day-recipes-appetizers-slow-cooker-crock-pot-2021-1">slow-cooker</a> Buffalo chicken dip is guaranteed to be the MVP at any party.</p><p>Practically every time I entertain friends — be it for <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/easy-air-fryer-recipes-game-day-appetizers">game day</a>, the Super Bowl, or any party — I'm always asked if I'll be making my famous Buffalo chicken dip.</p><p>Over the years, I've tweaked recipes I've seen online to come up with the easiest, most crowd-pleasing dip. It requires only six main ingredients, plus seasonings you'll probably already have in your pantry.</p><p>Here's how to make my <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/best-slow-cooker-comfort-food-recipes">easy slow-cooker</a> Buffalo chicken dip.</p><div id="slideshow"><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">My recipe for slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip requires only six main ingredients.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838a9fd3c7faef0ecd9c2b?format=jpeg" height="2304" width="3072" charset="" alt="slow cooker buffalo chicken dip ingredients"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>To make the dip, which feeds about 10 people, you'll need:</p><ul><li>A 6-quart slow cooker or Crock-Pot</li><li>A rotisserie chicken (or 1 lb of cooked chicken)</li><li>12 fluid ounces Frank's RedHot Buffalo sauce</li><li>½ cup ranch dressing</li><li>16-ounce cream cheese</li><li>1 cup shredded cheddar cheese</li><li>1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese</li><li>Salt, pepper, garlic powder</li></ul></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I always start by separating the breasts from the rotisserie chicken and removing the skin.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838aaea645d1188188ad86?format=jpeg" height="1982" width="2643" charset="" alt="rotisserie chicken"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I like to use rotisserie chicken for this recipe because it's often easier and cheaper than buying chicken breasts and boiling them myself. I find that the rotisserie chicken also packs much more flavor, and saves me from having to do any actual cooking.</p><p>When it comes to game-day recipes, easiest is usually best.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">Then I shred the rotisserie chicken.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838abaa645d1188188ad8b?format=jpeg" height="2304" width="3072" charset="" alt="shredded rotisserie chicken"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I usually do this step by hand, but you can also use two forks to shred your chicken. By the end, you should have about 3 cups of shredded rotisserie chicken.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I put the cream cheese in the slow cooker and cut it into cubes with a knife.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838ac7e1ba468a96ab6472?format=jpeg" height="2304" width="3072" charset="" alt="cream cheese in crock pot"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>This helps ensure the cream cheese melts evenly and is well-distributed throughout the dip.</p><p>You can use full-fat or low-fat cream cheese for this dip, depending on your preference — I've had success using both.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I then add the rotisserie chicken to the slow cooker and season it.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838ad5a645d1188188ad92?format=jpeg" height="2069" width="2759" charset="" alt="slow cooker buffalo chicken dip"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I usually eyeball how much seasoning I use, but typically go for about a tablespoon of garlic powder, a tablespoon of salt, and a few dashes of pepper.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I add the two types of cheese.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838af0e1ba468a96ab647d?format=jpeg" height="2146" width="2862" charset="" alt="slow cooker buffalo chicken dip"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I use 1 cup of shredded, low-moisture mozzarella cheese and 1 cup of shredded sharp-cheddar cheese.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">Next, my wet ingredients go on top.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838afdd3c7faef0ecd9c3f?format=jpeg" height="2123" width="2830" charset="" alt="slow cooker buffalo chicken dip"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I use a whole 12-ounce bottle of Frank's RedHot Buffalo sauce, but you can use whichever brand of Buffalo sauce you prefer. I then add ½ cup of ranch dressing on top.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I mix the ingredients with a wooden spoon until everything is evenly distributed.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69838b0ee1ba468a96ab6484?format=jpeg" height="2203" width="2938" charset="" alt="slow cooker buffalo chicken dip"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>You don't need to overmix it — as the dip cooks, the ingredients will melt and combine.</p><p>Scoop along the sides to make sure nothing is sticking to the walls, put the lid on the slow cooker, and walk away. It's that easy.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I heat the dip on high for 1 to 2 hours, or on low for 3 hours.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6983a30fe1ba468a96ab67bc?format=jpeg" height="2304" width="3072" charset="" alt="finished buffalo chicken dip in slow cooker"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I stir the dip with a wooden spoon a couple of times while it's cooking to prevent any spots from burning on the side and to help it cook evenly.</p><p>The dip should be smooth and slightly bubbling when it's done, with all the cream cheese and cheeses fully melted and combined.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I serve the finished Buffalo chicken dip with tortilla chips.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6983a3d3e1ba468a96ab67ec?format=jpeg" height="2304" width="3072" charset="" alt="tortilla chip dipped in buffalo chicken dip"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Erin McDowell/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>Whether you're making it for the Super Bowl, a last-minute party, or an easy weeknight snack, this six-ingredient slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip shows that crowd-pleasing food doesn't have to be complicated.</p><p>Simply toss everything in, let it cook, and you'll end up with a creamy, spicy dip that disappears almost as fast as it comes together.</p></div></div></div><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/easy-recipe-slow-cooker-buffalo-chicken-dip-game-day">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T13:12:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">I make the same Buffalo chicken dip recipe for every game day. It takes only six ingredients.</summary>

    <title>Half the drones in a recent US Army combat exercise were designed to be expendable like ammo</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T13:52:47Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/half-of-drones-at-us-army-exercise-were-expendable-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad87ab6794a2984cfca9d8?format=jpeg" height="3946" width="5919" alt="A US Army soldier conducts maintenance on a large fixed-wing drone in a forest."><figcaption>The war in Ukraine has shown the value of soldiers having a lot of drones they can expend without worrying about replacing them.<p class="copyright">US Army photo by Staff Sgt. Trevin Rund</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>US Army soldiers used about 2,000 attack drones in a recent exercise.</li><li>Half of those systems were designed to be consumable and used like ammunition.</li><li>Army officials and leaders have said small, low-cost drones are more useful in larger volumes.</li></ul><p>The US Army brought thousands of drones to a recent combat exercise, and roughly half were designed to be expendable. Soldiers could use and lose the drones in the fight, treating them like ammunition.</p><p>The Army's shift toward using <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/us-soldiers-working-out-how-to-use-drones-punishing-conditions-2026-8">low-cost drones</a> has relied on amassing enough systems to make them expendable. It's getting tens of thousands of drones to soldiers through the Drone Dominance Program, the goal being that soldiers use these systems without worrying about quickly coming up empty.</p><p>At the recent Saber Junction exercise in Germany, Army soldiers used approximately 1,900 autonomous systems.</p><p>"Those numbers continue to increase every rotation, and we will continue to increase them in future rotations," Maj. Gen. Christopher Norrie, acting commander of US Army Europe and Africa, told reporters at a roundtable on Thursday, which Business Insider received a transcript of.</p><p>Of those roughly 2,000 drones used during the exercise, "1,000 were consumable," Brig. Gen. Terry Tillis, head of the 7th Army Training Command, said, adding that soldiers were using them "<a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/us-soldiers-need-lots-cheap-drones-use-ammo-army-commander-2026-6">like a munition</a>."</p><p>"They're fired, and then it's employing them in a matter to achieve effects on the battlefield," he said.</p><p>At the Saber Junction exercise, US soldiers used <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/us-army-new-technology-combat-training-2026-9">drones in different combat scenarios</a>, some informed by the war in Ukraine, against electronic warfare and counter-drone systems. Army officials said replicating more challenging environments was important for giving soldiers realistic experiences.</p><p>Using a bunch of drones was similarly important, as "those drones are now a part of our basics of being able to survive and integrate into protection plans, using them to sense further and strike faster," Norrie said.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad88d716256d3825fdfa1b?format=jpeg" height="5464" width="6830" alt="Two US Army soldiers crouch in position with rifles in the forest."><figcaption>Other Army leaders have said drones are more of a niche capability if soldiers only have a few of them.<p class="copyright">US Army photo by SPC. Kaleb Lampkin</p></figcaption></figure><p>Russia's war in Ukraine has shown that while drones do not always replace more exquisite strike capabilities, they can offer soldiers a low-cost and effective method for hitting enemy targets. Not worrying about <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/us-army-mastering-drone-warfare-doesnt-mean-always-right-weapon-2026-2">losing the drones</a> to jamming or enemy fire — and having a large enough stockpile to resupply quickly — gives troops a fairly consistent weapon to rely on.</p><p>Last year, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth issued a memo directing an overhaul of how the Pentagon purchases small uncrewed aerial systems across the armed forces. The resulting program, Drone Dominance, is investing $1 billion to purchase at least 200,000 drones through 2027.</p><p>That memo also characterized how the military should be thinking small drones.</p><p>"Small UAS resemble munitions more than high-end airplanes. They should be cheap,rapidly replaceable, and categorized as consumable," the defense secretary wrote.</p><p>Tens of thousands of drones have been bought from different companies as part of the Drone Dominance effort. "We're in the process of receiving another 30,000 drones currently," Col. Gregory Merkl, the director of drone dominance for the Army, said. "That is enough absolutely to get them down to every squad level."</p><p>Soldiers have also been working on <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/more-than-half-army-brigades-one-way-drones-3d-printed-2026-6">building and 3D printing parts</a> for their own drones so that they can quickly craft systems when they need them or customize them for specific missions.</p><p>Earlier this year, a brigade from the 101st Airborne Division, for instance, assembled roughly 150 of the 228 attack drones they used in an exercise, with each system taking a couple of hours for a soldier to build.</p><p>Speaking about that exercise, Col. Ryan Bell, the commander of the 3rd Mobile Brigade, said, "If a company has only one or two drones, or a platoon has a single drone, it's a niche capability," Bell said, referring to one-way attack drones. "But a company that is provided 20 drones a day has an entirely new form of combat power."</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/half-of-drones-at-us-army-exercise-were-expendable-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T12:47:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">Army leaders have said that only a few drones present soldiers with a niche capability, while having more increases combat power.</summary>

    <title>I stayed at a Chicago hotel that was once a Gilded Age men's club. The history drew me in, but playful details won me over.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T12:10:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/chicago-athletic-association-hotel-review-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a91eb6445e6f385a516a799?format=jpeg" height="3750" width="5000" alt="Ornate lobby with gold coffered ceiling, marble columns, chandeliers, staircases, and black-and-white checkered floor."><figcaption>The Chicago Athletic Association is a hotel that was once an ultra-exclusive gentlemen&#39;s club. Business Insider&#39;s reporter booked a stay.<p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>When I checked in at the Chicago Athletic Association, I felt transported to the Gilded Age.</li><li>But that was just the beginning of my stay at the 19th-century private club turned hotel.</li><li>Parts of the hotel appeared frozen in time, while others breathed new life into its history.</li></ul><p>I've never been good at sports, and I've never been fond of exercise, so you might be wondering why I chose the Chicago Athletic Association when <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/avoid-when-booking-all-inclusive-vacation-mistakes-2026-1">booking hotels</a> for my first-ever trip to the city.</p><p>I wanted to step back in time. The <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/i-stayed-at-florida-gilded-age-hotel-vanderbilts-duponts-2025-7">Gilded Age hotel</a> was a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/new-gilded-age-everything-private-club-wealth-gyms-restaurants-2026-6">private club</a> where professional athletes and high-profile individuals trained and socialized from 1893 to 2007.</p><p>Following its closure and a lengthy transformation project, the Chicago Athletic Association reopened as a hotel in 2015. I spent one night there in February for $250. It felt extremely luxurious for the price point, and some surprising details made me certain I'd book it again.</p><p>Parts of my stay felt like a time warp, but the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/fairmont-le-chateau-frontenac-quebec-city-canada-hotel-review-photos-2022-9">hotel's history</a> also came out in ways I didn't see coming.</p><div id="slideshow"><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">Welcome to the Chicago Athletic Association, the 19th-century private club that&#39;s now a hotel.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fa5f415edd94d1e73398da?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="The exterior of the Chicago Athletic Association"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>The Venetian-Gothic-style building was designed by architect and club member Henry Ives Cobb, who took inspiration from the Doge's Palace in Venice, according to <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.chicagoathletichotel.com/hotel-history/">the hotel's website</a>.</p><p>The hotel stood out to me among modern buildings on Michigan Avenue in Downtown Chicago. It's just across from Millennium Park and the Bean (formally known as Cloud Gate) and within walking distance of many <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/us-tourist-attractions-worth-visiting-from-frequent-traveler-2026">tourist hot spots</a> like the Art Institute of Chicago, the Chicago Theater, and the Chicago Riverwalk.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">Inside, the past lives on.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fb9b30e1443b8dc48e2817?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="A wooden glass case displays historical facts and relics from the Chicago Athletic Association"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>The Chicago Athletic Association began as a Gilded Age gentlemen's club joined by influential sports icons. Membership opened to women in 1972.</p><p>It was a stomping ground for industry moguls like William Wrigley and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/richest-americans-in-history">Marshall Field</a>. It was a training base for five-time Olympic gold-medal swimmer Johnny Weissmuller and the first professional football player, William "Pudge" Heffelfinger.</p><p>The building's history is celebrated inside the hotel, with 19th-century relics and refurbished materials, from wood paneling to marble flooring, Elizabeth Story, the hotel's sales and marketing director, told Business Insider.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">As I stepped into the lobby, I felt like I&#39;d traveled back in time.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fb8fd5e1443b8dc48e27a6?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="Inside the dimly lit hotel lobby with dark, wooden detailing"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>The lobby, also known as the drawing room, looked as if it had been designed 100 years ago, with restored 19th-century trim, moldings, and replicated historic details.</p><p>"Teams of craftsmen restored the 1893 grandeur of the Lobby Lounge by removing, refinishing, and reinstalling every piece of millwork, and recreating original light fixtures from old photographs," Story said.</p><p>I noticed other contemporary details that pay tribute to the city and club's history. The check-in desk, designed with long strips of wood in different colors, was inspired by vintage athletic equipment.</p><p>"A mural above the desk depicts the elevated train tracks that encircle Chicago's Loop," Story added.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">Restored Gilded Age interiors made communal spaces look as lavish as they were historic.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fb8f0ac9dd4cb81cda7caf?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="Inside the hotel, a grand marble staircase at the back of a bright, empty hall with gold moldings on the ceilings"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I was mesmerized by the preserved luxury finishings as I walked through the hotel. Restored Italian columns, stained-glass windows, and golden doors made me feel as if I were inside a palace.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">The ballrooms had an old-world, luxury feel.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8f37b83f7df8787cff3d21?format=jpeg" height="1406" width="1875" charset="" alt="Ornate historic interior with stained-glass windows, carved wood paneling, marble floor, decorative ceiling, and lit fireplace."><figcaption><p class="copyright">Chicago Athletic Association</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>The hotel had many event spaces, including the White City Ballroom. During the restoration process, Story said that the Italian Carrara marble floor was buried under an inch and a half of carpet, glue, and concrete.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">I was surprised by another event space that used to be a swimming pool.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a96dde945e6f385a516b6d2?format=jpeg" height="1667" width="2500" charset="" alt="Empty grand interior hall with marble columns, ornate ceiling lighting, and a large roundel design on the floor."><figcaption><p class="copyright">Chicago Athletic Association</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>Known as "The Tank," this space still has the swimming lane flooring tiles from its pool days.</p><p>"Artists hand-made 167 individual stalactites as part of the atmospheric design," Story said.</p><p>Although the highlight of this room is the historic pool tiles, I thought repurposing the space for events was surprising and innovative.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">The game room had a mix of historic and fresh details.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fb9bb8e1443b8dc48e281f?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="Inside an empty game room with a foosball table in the foreground"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>The game room was the billiards room back in the club days, Story said.</p><p>It didn't feel frozen in time like some of the other spaces. The walls blended antique woodwork with whimsical murals, such as chalkboard sketches of athletes and an aerial view of a basketball court. I thought it was a playful, creative way to showcase the building's history.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">Some aspects of the hotel were completely new, like the rooftop bar and restaurant.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fba3223cfefc31768d656f?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="Inside an empty restaurant dining room with windowed ceilings"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>"The past was honored at every turn, but the transformation also called for thoughtful new additions," Story explained.</p><p>For example, Cindy's, the rooftop restaurant and bar, was built ahead of the hotel's 2015 opening.</p><p>I thought the space had a midcentury modern vibe with vintage influence. Cindy's brought the outdoors in with a steel-framed, windowed pavilion inspired by 19th-century train sheds.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">The fitness center was sleek and modern.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fba37ae1443b8dc48e2899?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="Cardio machines in the gym at the Chicago Athletic Association"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>Here, I found cardio machines with tablet attachments and fun cartoons of men stretching on the walls. The fitness center is open 24 hours a day.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">My room had a vintage aesthetic without feeling dated.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fb9c49e1443b8dc48e2829?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="Inside a room at the Chicago Athletic Association, there's a bed in between two nightstands and two windows on the left wall"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>I booked a standard room with a comfy king-sized bed and a downtown view for about $250 a night. I immediately noticed the custom metal bedframe with brass accents — a vintage design inspired by the 19th-century club.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">The furniture creatively combined elements of old-fashioned gym equipment in a functional way.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fba3b5e1443b8dc48e28a0?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="A desk, TV, and bar in front of the bed in the hotel room"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>The desk was unlike any I'd seen before. Wooden bars, inspired by stretching racks, climbed the wall to a netted shelf that appeared large enough to hold a typical checked suitcase.</p><p>The bars were cleverly used as vertical storage, with leather pouches of varying sizes hanging from them. I used these pockets to store my wallet, keys, and chargers during my stay.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">The bathroom blended old-school locker room vibes with opulence.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fba18fe1443b8dc48e2879?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" charset="" alt="A composite image of the hotel bathroom seen from two angles"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>"The bathrooms were conceived as a quiet luxury counterpoint," Story said. A black-and-white palette and a simple striped backsplash were paired with a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/carrara-marble-quarries-italy-what-its-like-to-visit-photos-2023-9">Carrara marble</a> vanity and a rainfall shower.</p><p>There was also a boxing-style robe in the bathroom, which almost made me feel like an athlete myself.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">At the Chicago Athletic Association, I got my trip back in time, with some surprises.</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/69fba4af3cfefc31768d657f?format=jpeg" height="3000" width="4000" charset="" alt="Inside the hotel, there are intricate moldings on the walls and elevators on the right"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Joey Hadden/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>While parts of the hotel felt 100 years old, fresh designs inspired by its private-club past gave other spaces a modern twist.</p><p>"The goal was never a museum-quality freeze in time, but something more alive," Story said. "A touch of disorder in the new space was introduced to draw in a younger generation, balanced bravely with references to the building's past."</p><p>From the palace-like common spaces to the creative nods to the past, the Chicago Athletic Association was more luxurious and distinctive than I expected for $250 a night. I would definitely stay there again, and maybe next time, I'll bring a jock with me.</p></div></div></div><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/chicago-athletic-association-hotel-review-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T12:10:01Z</published>

    <title>I left New York, moved to Boston, and had 3 kids. Along the way, I built a career that looks nothing like the one I planned.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T12:07:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-from-nyc-boston-had-kids-while-building-career-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad4f5416256d3825fdf73d?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" alt="composite image, on the right is the author working at a laptop with a baby on her lap, on the left the author is standing in front of a tree with her two kids"><figcaption>The author pictured a completely different career for herself when she was young.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Jenn Sinrich</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>I always wanted to work at magazines, but when I did, it wasn't quite what I imagined.</li><li>I wanted to write more, and went freelance. Then, my husband and I moved from New York to Boston.</li><li>While building our family, I also built a career I love.</li></ul><p>As a teenager, I'd sit on my bed flipping through glossy magazines, fascinated and completely absorbed by the empowering stories about women. The news felt dominated by men, but magazines seemed to offer a different world — one where women's lives, bodies, careers, and opinions were worthy of entire pages. I knew from an early age I wanted to help bring more of those stories to life.</p><p>In 2012, after studying journalism at Northeastern University, I <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-nyc-at-22-lived-with-70-year-old-roommate-2026-8">moved to New York City</a> as quickly as I could, interning at <em>Ladies' Home Journal</em> and <em>Self</em>, then gravitating toward parenting publications including<em> What To Expect, American Baby, </em>and <em>Fit Pregnancy.</em></p><p>Motherhood fascinated me long before I <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/what-it-really-means-to-be-a-mother-today-2026-3">became a mother</a>. It was the same intrigue and interest that drew me to magazines — the power of women, what their bodies could do, and the enormity of the identity shift involved in raising a child. Writing about pregnancy and parenting somehow felt very natural to me, even when I understood both mostly in theory.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad4fba4a3706ac06f84c40?format=jpeg" height="990" width="1320" alt="the author standing in front of a wall that says &quot;everyday health&quot;"><figcaption>The author decided to go freelance so she could write more.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Jenn Sinrich</p></figcaption></figure><h2 id="3e504d6e-a1fb-4d4f-a3d1-c92f9e97c80b" data-toc-id="3e504d6e-a1fb-4d4f-a3d1-c92f9e97c80b">I loved editing, but I wanted to write</h2><p>Working at magazines wasn't quite how I'd imagined it from my <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-to-make-childhood-bedroom-look-better-from-interior-designer-2022-12">childhood bedroom</a>. I loved editing: finding the heart of a story, moving pieces around, and helping a writer say what they were trying to say. My boss, Mindy, was one of the first people to make me believe that my creativity and instincts were worth trusting. She taught me nearly everything I knew about shaping a narrative.</p><p>But I also began to feel restless. I was putting so much of myself into stories that ultimately ran under somebody else's name. I longed for that authorship and craved the terrifying privilege of starting with a blank page, figuring out what I had to say, and hoping it might matter to even one reader.</p><p>Mindy warned me that <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/freelance-career-stable-treat-work-job-hunting-2026-6">freelancing would be hard</a>. I believed her and quit anyway. I had just gotten engaged, was planning a wedding, and was already thinking about having children. I also knew that if I kept waiting to feel established enough to become a writer, I might spend my entire career editing other people's work.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad4fe44a3706ac06f84c44?format=jpeg" height="2316" width="3088" alt="the author and her cat sitting in front of a laptop"><figcaption>The author ended up making more as a freelancer than at her 9-5.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Jenn Sinrich</p></figcaption></figure><p>I was scared to give up a steady paycheck, especially while planning a wedding and thinking about starting a family. Dan, my now-husband, understood the risk but supported me taking the chance. Neither of us knew whether I could make a sustainable living on my own; I only knew I would regret it if I didn't try.</p><p>The transition happened faster than I expected. Within the first few months, I had more assignments than I knew what to do with, partly because leaving my 9-to-5 meant I could attend daytime events, meet editors, and build relationships that led to more work. My income still varied from month to month, but it was far steadier than I had feared. By my second year of freelancing, I was writing at an almost ridiculous pace for around 20 magazines and websites and earning nearly four times the roughly $30,000 salary I'd once made as an editorial assistant.</p><p>My career became so much bigger after I left my staff job, but it looked so different from what I could have imagined.</p><h2 id="fb839bd5-474b-4d5f-9ec5-a340e57ab15a" data-toc-id="fb839bd5-474b-4d5f-9ec5-a340e57ab15a">Moving home changed the picture completely</h2><p>Life started looking even more different in 2018, about a year after I began freelancing, when my <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/unemployed-husband-lost-confidence-wife-support-2024-12">husband lost his job</a>. Because I didn't have employer-sponsored health insurance of my own, I had been covered through his job, so we lost coverage along with his paycheck. Our lease was also ending, and we wanted to start a family. Leaving New York suddenly felt less like giving something up and more like the only decision that made sense.</p><p>We moved to my hometown north of Boston, where my parents and oldest friends still lived. I became a mom the following spring, April 2019. Less than a year later, COVID turned the world upside down, and there wasn't a single person whose life looked the way they had imagined it.</p><p>My working life went from events, meetings, and crowded New York sidewalks to writing alone in the corner of a small, old house, albeit with an ocean view. There were no coworkers nearby, no glossy proofs circulating, and no one across the desk to bounce an idea off. There was just me, my laptop, my cat, and, during several stretches, a pregnant belly.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad50104a3706ac06f84c45?format=jpeg" height="3577" width="5365" alt="the author, her husband, and three kids standing on dunes at a beach wearing light clothing"><figcaption>The author and her husband now have three kids.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Jenn Sinrich</p></figcaption></figure><h2 id="71326f11-6d69-4403-b73e-9293349789d4" data-toc-id="71326f11-6d69-4403-b73e-9293349789d4">My hardest experiences became part of my work</h2><p>Motherhood was so different from what I'd imagined, and so was my path through it. While trying to grow my family, I suffered two miscarriages, which drastically changed the way I understood pregnancy, loss, and the motherhood journey in its entirety. I was so fortunate to have two healthy pregnancies afterward, but I couldn't shake everything the process had shown me.</p><p>I was inspired more than ever to create — to bring to life the kinds of platforms and communities I'd needed myself. I co-founded <a target="_blank" href="https://www.miscarriagemovement.com/">Miscarriage Movement</a>, to make pregnancy loss feel less isolating, as well as <a target="_blank" href="https://themotherchapter.com/">The Mother Chapter</a> to talk honestly about motherhood, identity, mental health, and ambition. Neither platform was part of a careful business plan. Both grew from experiences and questions I couldn't leave alone.</p><p>My career today looks nothing like the one I imagined as a teenager. I miss parts of New York and the collective energy of a magazine office. Freelancing can still be unpredictable, and running my own platforms means the work is never exactly finished. But I get to write, edit, create, and build something that belongs to me. I'm also <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/lived-with-parents-adult-now-neighbors-benefits-2026-7">close to my parents </a>and present for the small, ordinary parts of my children's lives.</p><p>The magazines on my childhood bed made me want to tell women's stories. All these years later, that's still very much what I'm doing. I just couldn't have imagined where I'd be doing it — or how much of my own life would eventually find its way onto the page.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-from-nyc-boston-had-kids-while-building-career-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I'm living in a 150-square-foot converted garage at my parents' house. They're helping me through a rough transition.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T11:41:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/living-in-converted-garage-parents-house-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad70954a3706ac06f84dc1?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" alt="Split interior view shows a mirror selfie over a decorated dresser and a compact room with bunk bed and kitchenette."><figcaption>The author is living in a converted garage at her parents&#39; house.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Camilla Richardson</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>I'm living in my parents' converted single-car garage, a roughly 150-square-foot casita.</li><li>While I'm separating from my husband, they've offered me more support than I ever expected.</li><li>Living close to them is helping me through this transition.</li></ul><p>In mid-August, I moved out of the home I shared with my husband. My new temporary home is my parents' <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/airbnb-two-car-garage-massachusetts-2025-6">converted single-car garage</a>, a roughly 150-square-foot casita.</p><p>I have asked for a divorce, although we haven't filed anything yet, so I'm still getting used to saying that word. My marriage had reached a point where I knew I needed to leave.</p><p>Friends offered me places to stay, but my parents are both <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/adult-relationship-with-parents-individuals-2024-2">in their early 70s</a>, and I wanted to spend time with them. However, the idea of living together still scared me. Our relationship was especially rocky around the time I left home as a teenager, when I vowed I would never live with them again.</p><p>We've all changed and grown in the 20 years since. I've matured and gained perspective with age, and they've softened and become more introspective. The casita also offers more privacy than living in my old bedroom would. Still, I worried <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-back-into-childhood-home-adult-30s-living-with-parents-2026-8">moving back home</a> would return us to those old dynamics, but it's only been a gift.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad713d16256d3825fdf8c9?format=jpeg" height="2048" width="2731" alt="sofa in front of a window in converted garage"><figcaption>The author has a sofa and a bunk bed in her space.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Camilla Richardson</p></figcaption></figure><h2 id="6e7b364d-6ee6-4c64-ae88-3d7b16d5a06f" data-toc-id="6e7b364d-6ee6-4c64-ae88-3d7b16d5a06f">Living in such a small space has challenges</h2><p>The casita is about 10 feet by 15 feet, and an adult life does not fit neatly into that square footage. But in reality, it's enough. It holds a bunk bed, a sofa, a kitchenette, a dresser, and a small bathroom. There's even a little portable island for me to sit at, though I use it to hold books and paperwork at the moment. Laundry and cleaning supplies are accessible in the main house, but my trips over are most often to <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/lived-with-parents-whole-life-benefits-downsides-helped-our-relationship-2026-8">spend time with my parents</a> rather than for practical reasons.</p><p>I'm still moving belongings out of my house and deciding what deserves a spot here. I've <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-to-clean-your-closet-tips-professional-organizer">downsized my clothes</a> and cleared out makeup and skincare products I wasn't using. My book collection is harder to cull; I love my books, and haven't figured out what to do about that yet.</p><p>The room was already furnished when I moved in, and we swapped a wardrobe for a more practical clothing rack; my mom donated the former, along with some shelves, to make space. I didn't even have to ask. My parents haven't imposed a laundry schedule, and they've made room for me without making me feel like an inconvenience.</p><p>I was especially worried about my <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/reference/chronic-headache">chronic migraines</a> during the move. I had arranged my previous home around them, including installing blackout curtains for days when the light is painful. Thankfully, my mother's decor already included blackout curtains, too. Sound and food smells can also be difficult during an attack, but the casita has an outside entrance and is separate enough that neither has been an issue. I'm only steps from my parents, but I still have privacy.</p><p>They aren't charging for rent or utilities while I figure out my finances during these transitional months. Hearing how much they love having me here is a balm as I go through this season.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad70d816256d3825fdf8c6?format=jpeg" height="3024" width="4032" alt="small converted garage with room for a bunk bed, dresser, and kitchenette"><figcaption>The author has made the most of the 150-square-foot space.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Camilla Richardson</p></figcaption></figure><h2 id="674a947c-527f-4a1b-8995-d70595c867f7" data-toc-id="674a947c-527f-4a1b-8995-d70595c867f7">My parents have supported me in ways I didn't expect</h2><p>Most nights, we <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/family-dinner-every-night-only-time-together-2026-6">eat dinner together</a>. I also sit with my dad while he feeds the neighborhood kittens that appear each day. They seem a little feral, but they love him. As soon as they hear his high-pitched call of "Kitty, kitty, kitty," they come running because they know it means food. I wouldn't see these ordinary moments if I had accepted a friend's spare room.</p><p>My parents are softer and more easygoing than I remember. They listen when I need to talk about my marriage. Recently, I saw that my husband had <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/husband-lost-wedding-ring-antigua-treasure-hunter-metal-detector-found-2026-5">taken off his wedding ring</a> when I came to visit our dog. I was still wearing mine out of respect for the fact that we are legally married and are only beginning this process. I asked for the divorce, but seeing his bare hand still hurt.</p><p>When I came home and cried, my parents listened. Growing up, they took care of all of my physical needs. Somehow, I feel more supported by them now. Their willingness to sit with me in the sadness means more than anything they could buy or fix.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad71664a3706ac06f84dc8?format=jpeg" height="3905" width="2742" alt="a window showing a view of sunflowers"><figcaption>She can see her mom&#39;s garden from her window.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Camilla Richardson</p></figcaption></figure><h2 id="d71355a8-7eb2-471f-8bc1-147fcd5b1024" data-toc-id="d71355a8-7eb2-471f-8bc1-147fcd5b1024">The casita is giving me time to figure out what I want next</h2><p>I see this as a transitional space. I don't know where I will live next or exactly how the <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/getting-divorced-advice-attorney-2018-12">divorce process</a> will unfold. Moving to my childhood home has become one of the kindest parts of an extremely painful time.</p><p>I had stopped expecting my relationship with my parents to feel this different. Living here has shown me that people can change, on both sides, even after you've given up imagining another version of the relationship. That means so much more to me than square footage.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/living-in-converted-garage-parents-house-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T11:41:01Z</published>

    <title>I thought I wanted the American dream. Moving to a small city in Spain changed my mind.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T11:20:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-north-carolina-to-spain-valencia-american-dream-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad39fc4a3706ac06f84b57?format=jpeg" height="2736" width="3648" alt="Kevin Joseph wearing sunglasses in a courtyard before a historic domed stone building in Simat de la Valldigna."><figcaption>Kevin Schreck in Simat de la Valldigna.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of  Kevin Schreck</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Kevin Schreck moved from a small town in North Carolina to Valencia, Spain, for a teaching program.</li><li>Schreck expected a short stay, but fell for Valencia and does not plan to return to the US.</li><li>He told Business Insider that he feels safer and happier in Spain, and his life is more affordable.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kevin Schreck, a 33-year-old from North Carolina who moved to Spain in 2018. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I was pursuing a master's in Spanish when I met my husband, who was also working on his master's. He's <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moving-from-usa-to-spain-business-working-less-2025-8">from Valencia</a>, so when we finished our programs, I thought, "He's lived here for a couple of years, why don't I go ahead and try Spain?"</p><p>I applied to a Spanish program that places native English speakers in public schools as classroom language assistants. I got really lucky and was assigned to a school in Valencia.</p><p>At first, my plan was to live there for a couple of years, improve my Spanish, and then return to the US to become a language teacher. I imagined having the typical American dream, you know, a house with a big yard and all that. But I <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moving-from-the-us-to-spain-surprising-things-american-2026-9">fell in love with Spain</a>.</p><p>I have so many fond memories of my first year in Valencia. I was this guy from Wilmington, North Carolina, learning about a new culture, trying new foods, meeting a ton of people, and going out with my husband and his friends.</p><p>I know I'm lucky, and not everyone has that experience. It's easy to get disillusioned when you're in a new country and don't have a community. But having my husband with me allowed me to immerse myself. It gave me an advantage, an easier way in, and that's something I really appreciate now.</p><h2 id="6928b2bc-fb18-4241-b4aa-f482a96c37d5" data-toc-id="6928b2bc-fb18-4241-b4aa-f482a96c37d5">Now I'm getting my Spanish citizenship</h2><p>Moving abroad was pretty easy. The teaching program provided me with a student visa, so I didn't have to figure everything out on my own or work with lawyers.</p><p>I was earning €1,000 ($1,146) a month through the program. It wasn't an amazing salary, but it was fairly typical and enough to live on. At the time, my partner and I rented an apartment in a decent area for €700 ($802) a month, which we split, so I could cover my rent and bills and still save a little.</p><p>It took me three months to receive my first payment. I was a recent college graduate relying on my savings, so that period was really stressful. But in the end, it all worked out.</p><p>I stayed in the program for a couple of years, which also made it easier to renew my visa. Afterward, I was able to apply for permanent residency, and now <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moving-from-usa-to-spain-business-working-less-2025-8">I'm working on my citizenship.</a></p><h2 id="d7e54325-012e-4b45-b98b-95bd3aa050e7" data-toc-id="d7e54325-012e-4b45-b98b-95bd3aa050e7">There's a lot to do in Valencia</h2><p>There's a lot to love about Valencia. It's usually sunny, and it isn't a huge city. With just under a million people, it feels much less overwhelming than Barcelona or Madrid — especially for someone like me who comes from the rural South.</p><p>But I think the biggest thing for me is the culture itself. <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/surprising-things-about-moving-to-europe-from-us-barcelona-spain">Spain isn't a monoculture</a>; the North and South are totally different, and several languages are spoken across the country. I really connected with Valencian culture, and I've been able to make friends and feel like I fit in pretty well.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad400f6794a2984cfca666?format=jpeg" height="2736" width="3648" alt="Kevin Joseph, wearing sunglasses, stands above a rocky beach with clear blue waters and white coastal cliffs."><figcaption>Schreck at a beach in Spain.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Kevin Schreck</p></figcaption></figure><p>I live just outside the city center in a fairly small neighborhood, but I really like it. There are a couple of nice little squares, along with restaurants, bars, cafés, and green spaces.</p><p>Valencia is really accessible, and I think that's important for quality of life. It takes me less than 30 seconds to walk to the grocery store, and if I want to meet friends, I'm usually no more than a 10-or 15-minute walk away. I live really close to the metro, too, and can get to the airport in about 20 minutes.</p><p>My family back <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-back-to-small-town-after-living-city-hometown-2026-6">in North Carolina</a> drives 45 minutes into town just to go to a restaurant. Now I think about that, and I'm like, "Oh my goodness." I really don't miss it.</p><h2 id="30e4c3af-ba0f-4197-bd5c-3a9c73cbf54a" data-toc-id="30e4c3af-ba0f-4197-bd5c-3a9c73cbf54a">Daily life is affordable in Spain</h2><p>About four years ago, my husband and I bought a 592-square-foot flat for about €150,000 ($172,317). Our mortgage is €604 ($692) a month. We got really lucky because it happened right before the big housing boom. Housing here is definitely much more expensive now.</p><p>Life here is affordable. For groceries, we probably spend between €80 and €100 a week for two people. We usually go out about once a week, maybe on a Saturday, and it's not a super expensive place to eat. A decent dinner is usually around €25 per person, so I'd say I spend about €100 a month on going out — maybe a little more if drinks are involved.</p><p>Healthcare isn't expensive here either. <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/best-healthcare-systems-in-the-world-2012-6">Spain has a universal healthcare</a> system, and that makes a huge difference in my life. Because I'm in the public system, I don't have to worry about getting a bill or whether it's worth going to the doctor because of a copay.</p><p>Of course, nowhere is perfect. The hardest part — and this probably isn't unique to Valencia — is learning a new language and culture and adjusting to a different way of life. You have to rethink the things you once considered normal in your hometown.</p><p>In Spain, there are a lot of unspoken rules. It's not something you learn in the first six months. You slowly catch on as you get better at the language and meet more people. It definitely took me time.</p><h2 id="e06a42c2-731f-445d-b3e8-e3aef09d061a" data-toc-id="e06a42c2-731f-445d-b3e8-e3aef09d061a">I don't plan on moving back to the US</h2><p>For my friends and family, the idea of my <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-asheville-north-carolina-better-quality-of-life-2026-5">moving from North Carolina</a> to Spain probably seemed pretty crazy. Because I've always liked to travel, I think they assumed I'd be there for a year and then come back. I don't think anyone expected me to stay permanently.</p><p>But I'm really happy to be living in Valencia, and I definitely don't intend to move back to the US.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad3b916794a2984cfca633?format=jpeg" height="3464" width="4618" alt="Two smiling people take a selfie beside a waterfront fountain with palm trees and city buildings behind them."><figcaption>Schreck and his partner, José, during his teaching program.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Kevin Schreck</p></figcaption></figure><p>My life has really blossomed in Spain. <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://abroadinvalencia.com/">I've become a travel advisor</a>, and my husband and I are in the process of adopting a child.</p><p>While I don't think the education system here is the best in the world, I think raising a child here feels safer; we don't have to worry about things like school shootings. Also, this is a bilingual region, so our child would also have the opportunity to learn several languages. As a big language nerd, I find that a huge plus.</p><p>While I do miss things about the US, especially my friends and family, I think this is the right place for me. </p><p>It's funny to think back to 2018, when my plan was to just be in Spain for a while; now my life looks completely different.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-north-carolina-to-spain-valencia-american-dream-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T11:20:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">Kevin Schreck says his quality of life is better in Valencia, Spain. Housing is affordable, and he is less worried about medical bills.</summary>

    <title>My outdoorsy husband didn't want to take a baby and a toddler camping. I insisted — and regretted it by 2 a.m.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T11:17:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/camping-baby-toddler-husband-was-right-family-trip-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aa99d11ec15fe2d3cf17bb4?format=jpeg" height="3024" width="4032" alt="Girl on a hammock."><figcaption>The author went camping with her family, but it only lasted 36 hours.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>I convinced my reluctant husband to take our two young kids camping.</li><li>Mosquito bites and the summer heat kept our toddler awake and miserable.</li><li>We abandoned the trip after 36 hours but decided to try camping again.</li></ul><p>The first sign that our family <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/best-camping-tips-for-first-timers-2021-11">camping trip</a> was a bad idea was that my husband and I were fighting. </p><p>Although he was a rugged outdoorsman who took frequent solo kayaking expeditions in the wilderness, he hated dragging our two kids into the woods in the peak of summer heat and <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/west-nile-triple-e-mosquito-virus-diseases-us-2024-9">mosquito season.</a></p><p>I disagreed. I'd only discovered a love for the outdoors as an adult, but I had a vision: our family playing in the water, me lounging by the lake in my sundress while the 13-month-old napped.</p><p>In truth, I had mid-summer anxiety and was desperate. Born in East Africa, I hated <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/midwesterners-love-winter-snow-reasons">Minnesota winters</a>. So I was frantic when I realized it was July and we hadn't moved beyond a 10-mile radius of our home. I wanted our family to make memories in the woods, and I wanted it now.</p><h2 id="1d691eae-fed6-4b53-8c8d-c4259ba53c7b" data-toc-id="1d691eae-fed6-4b53-8c8d-c4259ba53c7b">We went camping with our 2 kids</h2><p>Finally, he consented. He booked two nights in a state forest at the edge of the Boundary Waters, a massive forest on the border of Minnesota and Canada.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aa99fa6cc23a829a3b91dc2?format=jpeg" height="3024" width="4032" alt="Campsite"><figcaption>The author&#39;s husband set up the campsite.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><p>The next sign of trouble: we weren't prepared.  With three days to go before we left, we dashed around the city for essentials in 90-degree weather: a clunky fan from Cabela's and a screen shelter from the RV store (that turned out to be gazebo-sized and had to be replaced). I balked at the $100 <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/guides/home/stay-warm-at-kids-sports-events">camping chair</a> but added it to the cart anyway. Finding the right tent was a challenge. We had a two-person backpacking tent from life before kids. A no-go. Luckily, a friend lent us his tent. We packed enough for two weeks, and by the miracle of extra daylight, we were ready to go by Friday.</p><p>We arrived at the campsite. I slapped <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/mosquito-tick-repellent-bug-spray-2018-7">citronella spray</a> on my toddler's legs before she excitedly ran through the winding path from our campsite to the water. I followed her, and my daughters and I sat by the water, watching three boys hunt tadpoles. I didn't notice the bug bites she was getting, preoccupied with blocking the sticks my newly mobile infant was trying to sneak into her mouth.</p><h2 id="423d57df-cbc1-4916-86bb-32fc674d647c" data-toc-id="423d57df-cbc1-4916-86bb-32fc674d647c">The kids woke up at 2 a.m.</h2><p>We quickly learned that camping with young kids was just like parenting at home, only with fewer amenities, more dust, and no safe spot to park our infant. After dinner, while we were <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/cards-against-humanity-virtually-online-video-chat-how-to-play-2020-3">playing card games</a>, my toddler started complaining that her legs were itchy. I rubbed a balm from a tin with a badger on her. I was ill-equipped for what followed.</p><p>At 2 a.m., we woke to the kids' meltdown.  The bites were too itchy. The tent was too warm. The sheets irritating. I rubbed more balm. For an hour, she wailed as I hunted for stronger and stronger concoctions that weren't locked up in the car to prevent bears from wandering over.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aa9a0b2cc23a829a3b91dcf?format=jpeg" height="2268" width="3024" alt="Baby trying to get in the water"><figcaption>The author&#39;s family lasted 36 hours camping.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><p>Eventually, the baby woke up and needed to be nursed.</p><p>No amount of balm helped. We switched to distracting her and cooling her down. I stripped her down and cranked the fan on her legs while my husband told the world's longest story about the bear with no hair.</p><p>The next morning, our girl was keener to jump into the lake than to process how she felt. The cool water was both delightful and soothing. In good spirits, she made friends with the boulder by our campsite.</p><h2 id="25927840-85b6-49e0-a676-70fdc2af9e70" data-toc-id="25927840-85b6-49e0-a676-70fdc2af9e70">We left early</h2><p>Success, I thought, as I lounged at base while the baby napped in her Pack 'n Play. The park had running water, so at dinnertime, I suggested a cool shower to help the kids get ready for bed. The heat clung to our bodies, and I thought a rinse-off would help with sleep. We were nearly scalded. The tap had two settings: off or lava.</p><p>Within minutes, the bites flared up again. As she wailed, I looked into her bloodshot and unhappy eyes. I thought of spending another night in the cramped tent with paper-mache zippers while the mosquitoes hovered outside. I thought of another 3 a.m. therapy session to soothe my child. I thought of the rock that had lodged itself against my thigh as I slid around our 1-inch sleeping pads while tending to both kids. We were miserable.</p><p>"Let's pack up and go home," I told my spouse.</p><p>While I fed the kids yogurt bowls, my husband quickly stuffed everything into our car. Driving home with the kids soundly asleep, I looked out at the forest and the setting sun. A black bear poked its head up as we drove through empty roads. It was my first sighting.</p><p>Back in cell service, we stopped at the pharmacy and then gave our child Zyrtec before tucking her in.</p><p>"I feel like we've been gone for a week," my husband remarked as we collapsed on the Adirondack chairs on our front porch.</p><p>It should have been our last time attempting this madness. By all accounts, it was a flop. But our daughters played with sticks and water. Our toddler made friends with a rock. Our 36 hours of suffering had to be for something.</p><p>So a few weeks later, we cautiously tried again. This time: one night, shorter drive, better tent, pre-cooked meals, and lots of bug spray and long sleeves. We ran our Thermacell most of the day at camp. I actually sat in my new chair while we played Go Fish.</p><p>The kids splashed in a clear lake, played with sand, and slept soundly under the stars. As we drove home, our toddler asked, "Mama, when can we go back?"</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/camping-baby-toddler-husband-was-right-family-trip-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T11:17:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">Our first camping trip with two young kids ended after 36 hours. We tried again with better planning, and our toddler begged to return.</summary>

    <title>Stock compensation gives Big Tech workers a powerful reason to stay. Layoffs and the AI boom are changing the equation.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T10:30:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/big-tech-stock-compensation-golden-handcuffs-equity-google-apple-microsoft-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad3e264a3706ac06f84b89?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" alt="Rob Waters (left), Julie Zhu (center), and Yousuf Imran (right)"><figcaption>Rob Waters (left), Julie Zhu (center), and Yousuf Imran (right) weighed Big Tech stock compensation as they considered their next career moves.<p class="copyright">Rob Waters (left), Julie Zhu (center), and Yousuf Imran (right)</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Big Tech stock can be worth a fortune — if workers remain employed long enough to get it.</li><li>Layoffs can suddenly wipe out stock workers were waiting to collect.</li><li>The AI boom is creating another potential path to equity riches: joining a startup or building one.</li></ul><p>The day after Rob Waters learned of his layoff from Google last year, he was encouraged to apply for a new role there as an AI sales specialist. Google soon offered him the position, with a six-figure salary.</p><p>Waters wasn't sure he wanted to return. He'd grown frustrated with the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/google-bureaucracy-working-from-home-office-eric-schmidt-wfh-rto-2024-8">bureaucracy at Google</a> and how the reorganization that eliminated his team had been handled.</p><p>But walking away meant giving up about a few hundred thousand dollars in unvested equity.</p><p>"I killed myself working and dedicating myself, and then all I got to show for it was getting let go," said the 42-year-old, who lives in San Francisco.</p><p>He'd also dreamed of starting his own company. The layoff, he said, "ripped the bandaid off." Waters decided to bet on himself and pursue Kanawai AI, a startup he cofounded.</p><p>"All the equity that was unvested was gone," he said. "I went from making very high six figures to zero."</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aac4c116794a2984cfca21e?format=jpeg" height="806" width="1074" alt="Rob Waters"><figcaption>Rob Waters chose to pursue an AI startup rather than return to Google and continue vesting his equity.<p class="copyright">Rob Waters</p></figcaption></figure><p>Stock compensation has long given Big Tech workers a powerful incentive to stay put. Since the end of 2022, shares of Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft have all at least doubled.</p><p>But years of <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/life-lessons-from-big-tech-workers-who-got-laid-off-2026-8">Big Tech layoffs</a> have reminded some workers that their stock compensation isn't guaranteed. Meanwhile, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/google-employee-made-one-million-explains-why-left-big-tech2026-6">the AI boom</a> has created another path to potential equity riches. And for some workers, years of gains on vested stock have given them the financial security to leave Big Tech on their own terms.</p><h2 id="940b9899-5310-4fd9-9bcd-712494af9ecb" data-toc-id="940b9899-5310-4fd9-9bcd-712494af9ecb"><strong>When Big Tech stock makes leaving easier</strong></h2><p>Julie Zhu, 29, had wanted to <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/former-apple-employee-worked-13-hour-days-building-her-startup-2026-8">become a founder</a> since she was 18 and said she'd developed a "love-hate relationship" with Apple, where she worked as a product designer. She was grateful for what she'd learned at the company but said it was a high-pressure, high-stress environment. She wanted more control over her work.</p><p>Still, Zhu wanted to make sure she could afford the risk of leaving. Her goal was to have three to five years of runway. Her Apple stock came in handy.</p><p>"I didn't sell anything during my time at Apple, and Apple has been doing really well," she said.</p><p>Last year, after nearly four years at Apple, Zhu resigned to focus on Odd One In, the artist collectible company she'd been building on the side. She said it felt like the right time, though leaving meant forfeiting the remaining quarter of her Apple stock grant that hadn't yet vested.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aac4c7e16256d3825fdf265?format=jpeg" height="1701" width="2268" alt="Julie Zhu"><figcaption>Julie Zhu said her Apple stock helped give her the financial security to pursue entrepreneurship.<p class="copyright">Julie Zhu</p></figcaption></figure><p>Yousuf Imran also built up a financial cushion during roughly six years at Google, where his compensation included company stock. He set aside $350,000 for business and personal expenses before leaving in April to start an <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/google-employee-made-one-million-explains-why-left-big-tech2026-6">AI sales tools company</a>. Imran said the potentially "life-changing" equity packages at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic shaped his decision.</p><p>"If the only way to get real upside in this AI moment is equity, at some point, you ask yourself whether the equity should be in your own company," he said.</p><p>Dave Lewis also credited stock compensation for giving him the flexibility to consider career options outside Big Tech. Lewis, who spent more than a decade working at Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, said the wealth he'd accumulated from stock compensation gave him enough of a financial cushion to be selective after he was <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/laid-off-amazon-microsoft-millennial-tech-job-market-artificial-intelligence-2026-6">laid off by Microsoft</a> last October.</p><p>With AI reshaping the tech industry, Lewis said he wanted his next role to position him for where he thought the industry was headed. In May, he joined Emberos, an AI startup, as head of partnerships.</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. <strong>Share your story </strong>with him by <a target="_blank" rel=" nofollow" class="" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSechTVqVWQve8iqYssNriCXdtwwdgGRixNNZpmslSKBQqIJ8g/viewform?usp=header">filling out this form</a>, <a target="_blank" rel=" nofollow" class="" href="mailto:jzinkula@businessinsider.com">emailing him</a>, or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. <strong>Follow his work</strong> by <a target="_blank" rel=" nofollow" class="" href="https://lnkd.in/gPbQpyJn">clicking here</a>.</p>
      </aside>
    <h2 id="db876493-a949-41ae-b7e3-962e6eedcde0" data-toc-id="db876493-a949-41ae-b7e3-962e6eedcde0"><strong>With stock compensation, timing can be everything</strong></h2><p>For all its potential upside, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/quitting-big-tech-entrepreneur-stock-compensation-concentration-risk-2025-6">stock compensation</a> can leave workers' finances exposed to luck and timing: of when they join the company, vesting schedule, stock performance, and their decisions to sell or hold. One former Meta employee got lucky: Meta's shares had fallen sharply when he joined in 2022 and received a "boatload" of restricted stock units on the cheap. The stock then surged over the next few years.</p><p>Not everyone is as fortunate. A former Microsoft employee in her 60s said she still held a large amount of company stock when she lost her job last year after more than a decade there. She initially thought her savings and stock holdings might allow her to retire, but after Microsoft shares fell sharply, she began to question whether she could afford to.</p><h2 id="7043719f-46cf-49f9-b0b8-d55c56be0376" data-toc-id="7043719f-46cf-49f9-b0b8-d55c56be0376"><strong>The golden handcuffs only go so far</strong></h2><p id="e8702805-982c-4f72-97d2-edce8a629563">For all its complications, stock compensation remains one reason Big Tech is so appealing. A former Amazon employee said the company's salary-and-stock compensation was lucrative and also felt more predictable than the bonus-heavy pay structure she had at her previous employer.</p><p>But even a predictable compensation package depends on keeping the job. After a few years at Amazon, she was laid off last year.</p><p>Even for workers who do retain their jobs, the financial incentives to stay only go so far. As Bushra Amiwala weighed whether to leave her sales associate role to <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/gen-zer-quit-google-job-run-for-congress-big-tech-2026-3">run for Congress</a>, she said she felt the pull of Big Tech's so-called "<a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/big-tech-golden-handcuffs-become-silicon-rsus-nvidia-amd-broadcom-2025-10">golden handcuffs</a>." Staying at Google offered the salary, stock, and stability that could help her continue supporting her immigrant parents financially.</p><p>For Amiwala, the deciding question wasn't whether she'd win the race — she ultimately left Google but lost the election — or what she'd give up financially by leaving Google. It was whether, five or 10 years later, she'd regret not taking the chance.</p><p>"For me, it was a no-brainer," she said. "I knew I'd regret not doing it."</p><p><em>Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at </em><a target="_blank" href="mailto:jzinkula@businessinsider.com"><em><u>jzinkula@businessinsider.com</u></em></a><em>, or via Signal at jzinkula.29.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/big-tech-stock-compensation-golden-handcuffs-equity-google-apple-microsoft-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
