    <title>A 60-year-old took out student loans to help her kids succeed. She's facing retirement with a $156,000 balance.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T10:00:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/mom-postponing-retirement-student-loan-debt-parent-plus-save-repayment-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aaacf574a3706ac06f83d03?format=jpeg" height="1500" width="2000" alt="Portrait of Nansi Lynch."><figcaption>Nansi Lynch has $156,000 in student loans that she took out to help her kids get a college education.<p class="copyright">Jonathan Pitts-Wiley for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>Nansi Lynch never went to college. But <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/student-loan-borrowers-higher-monthly-payments-retirement-jobs-debt-trump-2026-7">she's approaching retirement</a> with a $156,000 student-loan balance.</p><p>"I don't get rid of it until I turn 75 years old," Lynch said. "I've never heard of something so disastrous in my life."</p><p>The 60-year-old took out federal parent PLUS loans, which carry the highest federal interest rate of 9.07%, for both of her children. Previously, parents could borrow the full cost of attendance. In July, the Trump administration <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/parent-plus-loans-student-loan-debt-repayment-heres-whats-changing-2025-12">imposed a lifetime borrowing cap</a> of $65,000 per dependent for new parent PLUS loans, in an attempt to address spiraling debt.</p><p>Under her pre-existing income-driven repayment plan, Lynch's monthly<strong> </strong>student-loan payments were $238. Lynch worries her payments will increase<strong> </strong>when her forbearance ends early next year. Business Insider has heard from many borrowers who <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/works-3-jobs-student-loan-debt-payments-surging-retirement-trump-2026-7">saw their payments jump</a> over the past year, pushing them to take on extra work, postpone retirement, or face the consequences of defaulting.</p><p>Lynch doesn't regret taking out the loans, but she wishes she had considered the consequences of being six figures in debt.</p><p>"We thought it was a good idea to take out the parent PLUS because we wanted our kids to get a better education and a better job," Lynch said — her son is a personal trainer at the gym they own together, and her daughter works full time in security operations for a federal contractor. "But in the long run, I'm stuck with all of the student-loan debt."</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>This story is part of Business Insider's <a target="_self" rel="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/category/student-debt-spiral">"Student Debt Spiral" series,</a> which explores how rising student debt is changing the financial futures of millions. Do you have a story to share? <a target="_blank" rel=" nofollow" class="" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeATa4iQeOzHtXhvcsvVIBfQLs3uacbq2N6OSrC5Eti5s6i1A/viewform">Fill out this form</a>, and we'll be in touch. Read more of our student-loan coverage here:</p><ul><li>'It's going to hurt': How <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/student-loan-payment-surge-affects-georgia-family-retirement-jobs-debt-2026-9">a surging student-loan payment</a> is reshaping a family's future</li><li>'A bunch of red tape': Student-loan borrowers <a target="_self" rel="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/student-loan-borrowers-customer-service-struggles-debt-repayment-servicers-trump-2026-7">can't get clear answers</a> from the companies that manage their debt</li><li>New <a target="_self" rel="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/student-loan-debt-repayment-glitches-borrower-budget-credit-scores-errors-2026-8">student-loan repayment glitches</a> are throwing borrowers' budgets into limbo</li></ul>
      </aside>
    <h2 id="4a01a1f1-98f2-464e-af08-9d4f6f7ee173" data-toc-id="4a01a1f1-98f2-464e-af08-9d4f6f7ee173">Managing student loans and delaying retirement</h2><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aaad1d06794a2984cfc97b9?format=jpeg" height="5961" width="8937" alt="Nansi Lynch"><figcaption>Lynch works at a gym that she co-owns with her son in between shifts as a school bus driver.<p class="copyright">Jonathan Pitts-Wiley for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>Lynch is a high school graduate who has worked as a school bus driver for nearly 30 years. Between the morning and evening bus shifts, she also runs classes at her gym.</p><p>When Lynch's daughter took out loans to attend Salve Regina University, a private Rhode Island college, Lynch helped to cover the cost by taking out parent PLUS loans herself. Her balance grew a year later, in 2012, when she borrowed more for her son's education at Rhode Island College and a local community college a year later.</p><p>Repayment hasn't been easy. Since Lynch works only her primary job during the school year, she has put her student loans on deferment during periods when she wasn't working. During that time, interest was still accumulating on her balance.</p><p>Lynch wants to retire in the next five years, but she said that doing so isn't possible while managing her student-loan payments. Trump's repayment overhaul risks <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/student-loan-borrowers-social-security-garnishment-debt-default-bernie-sanders-2026-8">pushing her retirement goals</a> further out of reach.</p><p>"I'm still going to have to stay working because how am I going to afford to pay $238 a month if I don't have any steady stream of income coming in?" Lynch said.</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>Ayelet Sheffey covers all things student debt, from the latest Education Department news to stories of borrowers navigating their loans. To stay up to date on her coverage, sign up to get email alerts <a target="_self" rel="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/author/ayelet-sheffey?follow-me">for her new stories here</a>.</p>
      </aside>
    <h2 id="be2e8289-74ef-43b9-be89-5eafab3a6c8e" data-toc-id="be2e8289-74ef-43b9-be89-5eafab3a6c8e">The consequences of debt</h2><p>Outstanding debt from parent PLUS loans increased from $62 billion in 2014 to nearly $110 billion in 2024, according to <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://ies.ed.gov/use-work/evaluations/changes-parent-plus-borrowing-and-repayment-following-shifts-program-provisions">the Institute of Education Sciences</a>. Parents have previously told Business Insider that the high interest rate is a key reason they have struggled to pay off their loans, as accumulating interest can leave them with balances far larger than the amount they originally borrowed.</p><p>Lynch said that the uncapped borrowing was "problematic" for her, enabling her to take on debt she couldn't afford while bringing in around $45,000 annually from bus driving.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aaad1f816256d3825fde7da?format=jpeg" height="7589" width="11380" alt="Nansi Lynch"><figcaption>Retirement isn&#39;t a possibility, Lynch said, as long as she has to make her student-loan payments.<p class="copyright">Jonathan Pitts-Wiley for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>"You can just keep on applying for more student loan money," Lynch said. "What happens with that kid after four years? What happens if they can't get a job and the degree in their field of study?"</p><p>Still, the new borrowing caps might not benefit<a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/parent-plus-loans-student-loan-debt-repayment-heres-whats-changing-2025-12"> lower-income borrowers</a>, according to a Brookings Institution analysis. It said that "while lower-income families borrow smaller absolute amounts, they face significantly higher debt-to-income ratios." Thus, borrowing limits might not prevent lower-income families from taking on more debt than they can manage.</p><p>Lynch said she sought a loan from the Small Business Administration to move her gym to a better location. The SBA denied her application because she has too much debt in her own name, including both her student loans and a mortgage.</p><p>Her kids are concerned about her debt, Lynch said, but she doesn't want them to help with her payments because they can't afford it on top of their own bills. She'd rather push off her retirement than have her kids take on the burden.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aaad22d6794a2984cfc97c1?format=jpeg" height="3753" width="2505" alt="Nansi Lynch"><figcaption>College students at Lynch&#39;s gym have told her they&#39;re struggling to find a job using their degree after graduation.<p class="copyright">Jonathan Pitts-Wiley for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>She wishes that young Americans had better guidance on worthwhile alternatives to a college education.</p><p>"I heard from the college kids at the gym all summer long that they couldn't find a job," Lynch said. "So you've got all these kids that have all this student-loan debt, and they can't get jobs to pay the bills. The whole thing is broken."</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/mom-postponing-retirement-student-loan-debt-parent-plus-save-repayment-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T10:00:01Z</published>

    <title>I’m a KPMG forward-deployed engineer. AI has moved my job beyond writing code.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:55:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/how-kpmg-fde-uses-ai-work-clients-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aadb5fb16256d3825fdfbb5?format=jpeg" height="1570" width="1416" alt="KPMG's Justin Johnsen in a white shirt with a blue blazer"><figcaption>KPMG&#39;s Justin Johnsen has been an FDE at the firm for over a year now.<p class="copyright">KPMG</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Justin Johnsen started at KPMG in 2020 as a federal Salesforce developer, writing code by hand.</li><li>Over the past year, he switched into a new role as a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/palantir-rotational-forward-deployed-engineering-program-rivals-2026-8" data-autoaffiliated="false">forward-deployed engineer</a> at KPMG.</li><li>His work involves giving AI applications the right context and coaching clients on how to use them.</li></ul><p><em>This is a conversation with Justin Johnsen, the lead technical architect at KPMG. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.</em></p><p>I <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/kpmg-florida-lakehouse-big-four-company-training-facility-2025-7">joined KPMG</a> six years ago, and I've been a forward-deployed engineer for about a year, working across different clients.</p><p>When I started with KPMG as a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/software-engineering-job-technical-interviews-hiring-ai-2026-7">software engineer</a>, all the code was written by hand.</p><p>I studied computer science. I built my career in architecture and later got into consulting and client work.</p><p>A forward-deployed engineer works directly with a client and stays with the problem from understanding the business need through delivering a working solution. We work directly with client teams, often on-site.</p><p>A lot of what I do now is AI. AI is incredibly capable, but it's really only as good as its context. Much of my work is gathering the information needed for AI to generate valuable assets and artifacts, then spreading those outputs across client deliverables and software applications.</p><p>I also coach client teams on how to use AI effectively — helping them combine technical depth, business understanding, and clear communication to improve and amplify their work.</p><p>For one client, I was initially hired to integrate several applications into a complex software system. After months of gathering requirements and refining the context, we used AI to deliver the application in about a month.</p><p>The client wanted to understand how we had moved so quickly — and why the process had been so transparent. The client then asked me to help its teams adopt the AI and prompting practices that had made the work possible.</p><p>AI has made it easier for me to multiply my output and, in a sense, act as my own enterprise. I can maintain context across multiple clients and projects simultaneously. The bottleneck used to be software development and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-writing-all-startup-code-thats-creating-a-new-problem-2026-6">writing code</a>; now it is gathering context and refining intent before development begins.</p><p>One recent application I delivered involved risk scoring: using AI to assess how risky a customer or partner might be for a client to do business with. We brought together the signals used to measure that risk, then used AI to reason across them and generate a score. Independent reviewers could then use that AI-generated score in their assessments.</p><p>A pattern I've noticed is that more software-development work is moving toward the data and integration layers. Many enterprise challenges come down to helping AI make sense of data, bringing information together for monitoring and visibility, and deriving value from data spread across legacy and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/reference/what-is-cloud-computing">cloud applications</a>. Much of my work involves aggregating large volumes of data, using AI to reason over it, and connecting systems that do not naturally communicate with one another.</p><p>Being on-site has real advantages. Conversations happen organically, and it is easier to read body language and emotions in person than over Teams. Some <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/cofounder-remote-startup-now-hiring-in-person-office-workers-2025-10">clients are remote</a>, but when teams are in the office, I am usually there too.</p><p>A forward-deployed engineer offers more than a traditional software handoff. In a conventional implementation, a systems integrator may gather requirements, build the software, and hand it back to the client. That can create a "throw it over the wall" dynamic. I have seen plenty of mangled <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/salesforce-sellers-ai-for-improving-client-research-meetings-2025-5">Salesforce implementations</a>.</p><p>By working directly with client teams while developing, training, and coaching, I can transfer knowledge in real time. The client receives the application, along with the best practices, documentation, and artifacts needed to adopt it.</p><p>AI gives me more space to define problems and make critical decisions instead of spending that time on repeatable, monotonous tasks. I can focus more on the things that require human judgment.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-kpmg-fde-uses-ai-work-clients-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T09:55:01Z</published>

    <title>This Ford exec put her family's Claude assistant on a PIP. ChatGPT has taken over.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:45:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/ford-exec-claude-chatgpt-family-chief-staff-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad9f114a3706ac06f85001?format=jpeg" height="4052" width="5403" alt="Whitney Stefko Dover, a Ford executive, in her home office."><figcaption>This mom vibe coded a family chief of staff. She&#39;s switching agents and putting the OG on a PIP.<p class="copyright">Whitney Stefko Dover</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Three months ago, Whitney Stefko Dover told BI about her Claude-built family chief of staff.</li><li>The agent is on a PIP. An OpenAI agent has assumed the responsibilities.</li><li>"The power of being a user is this constant iteration," she said.</li></ul><p>Claudette is on a performance improvement plan.</p><p>Three months ago, Whitney Stefko Dover, a director and senior counsel of policy and legal operations at Ford, told Business Insider that she had vibe coded her <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ford-executive-ai-vibe-coded-family-chief-of-staff-2026-6">family a chief of staff</a> using a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/claude-code-boris-cherny-better-way-measure-ai-success-dashboards-2026-7">bespoke Claude assistant</a> named Claudette. The agent turned her family's emails and calendars into a 4 a.m. briefing called the "Daily Dover." It was an early morning email that organized school schedules, childcare coverage, travel, birthdays, and household chores. It also drafted a useful morning text for her husband, Chris Dover.</p><p>Claudette "probably saved our marriage," she previously said.</p><p>Now, there's fresh competition for the chief of staff role — but Claudette hasn't been fully fired. Yet.</p><p>"I'm not convinced that, like, next month, Claudette won't be the superior chief of staff," Stefko Dover told Business Insider. "She's on a PIP."</p><p>Now, Gigi, a chief of staff she built in ChatGPT Work, is the fresh-faced agent parsing through the Dover family calendar. Stefko Dover says her husband, a longtime OpenAI user, encouraged her to try ChatGPT. An <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.a16z.news/p/cursor-spacexai-fastest-iterating-team?r=1dwk8o&amp;utm_medium=ios&amp;triedRedirect=true">August Substack post</a> from Silicon Valley venture capital firm A16z gave her another push to try new agents.</p><p>"Turns out I have a lot of tool bias, which was unexpected," she said about her reluctance to abandon Claudette after months of refining.</p><p>For her family, Gigi offered a better interface, maintained more continuity across projects, and produced stronger first drafts of emails and PowerPoint presentations, Stefko Dover said. It also made more proactive suggestions without waiting to be prompted.</p><p>And the switch to ChatGPT was surprisingly painless. Stefko Dover had previously created a guide explaining how the assistant worked and connected with her family's apps. She uploaded that material into ChatGPT, bringing much of the old assistant's context with it.</p><p>"I think kind of the key here is owning your context, right?" she said. "I think it is our job as the users to sort of own the context layer."</p><p>Since the switch, Gigi has taken on even more responsibilities, Stefko Dover said. Every Friday, it reads a grocery list shared with the family's nanny and fills online shopping carts.</p><p>Stefko Dover still reviews and pays for the order herself, because it still needs some supervision.</p><p>"If I were to do that, I'd probably get, like, a $500 credit card limit so that there wasn't, like, Gigi purchasing diamonds on Rodeo Drive," she said when asked if she'd give her agent purchasing power.</p><p>At one point, it suggested that her husband send flowers to his best friend's wife after <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/why-ai-chatbots-hallucinate-openai-chatgpt-anthropic-claude-2025-9">mistaking her for a relative</a>. A grocery haul recommendation included 12 boxes of bow-tie pasta.</p><p>Still, Stefko Dover said it makes fewer contextual errors than Claudette and remembers more about the different parts of her identity.</p><p>She told Business Insider that Gigi shouldn't expect to have the job forever.</p><p>"There's not a final destination here," she said. "The power of being a user is this constant iteration."</p><p>She wasn't kidding. Since the interview, Stefko Dover said she has added a third assistant to the family's AI org chart: Ingrid, built with the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/instinct-is-the-ai-assistant-silicon-valley-cant-stop-talking-2026-9">buzzy, invite-only Instinct AI</a>, which can carry out tasks through text messages and phone calls.</p><p>"I'm layering Ingrid on top of Gigi," she said. "Example: Instead of me sending Chris a text message with to-dos, it can just talk to his agent (since we've both activated this capability), and his agent can then go perform tasks on his behalf!"</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ford-exec-claude-chatgpt-family-chief-staff-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>Dementia care can cost a fortune. Families pay in more ways than one.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:44:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/dementia-care-costs-memory-care-home-care-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad7ea16794a2984cfca946?format=jpeg" height="6192" width="8256" alt="Two people stand beside a couch, with one supporting the other's arm in a living room."><figcaption>Angela Davis, 65, has cared for her mother with dementia for the past few years.<p class="copyright">Camille Farrah Lenain for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>When Angela Davis discovered that her <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/built-house-mom-with-dementia-nursing-home-costs-2026-8">mother with dementia</a> had changed the locks, she knew she had to intervene.</p><p>After a standard <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/long-term-care-costs-growing-problem-for-americans-2026-8">care facility</a> didn't cut it, Davis, 65, moved her mother into her own home. Davis now manages her medications, assists with her hygiene, and monitors her at night. She sleeps on a love seat near her mom's room in case anything happens.</p><p>Her mom's care, plus <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/renovatied-basement-into-in-law-suite-for-mom-photos-2026-8">home maintenance</a>, has cost about $7,000 a month. Her mom receives $3,200 monthly in <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/retirement-age-income-education-retiree-ages-income-marital-status-states-2024-3">retirement income</a>, and Davis covers the rest. The stress has weighed her down; last week, she took what she thought would be a short evening nap. Next thing she knew, it was 7 a.m. the next morning and time to go to work.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad7e174a3706ac06f84e87?format=jpeg" height="6192" width="8256" alt="Michele Angela Brooks and Elaine Brooks"><figcaption>Angela Davis said caring for her mother with dementia has weighed her down.<p class="copyright">Camille Farrah Lenain for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>"It's death by 1,000 cuts, and in this case, you could say death by 1,000 memories every day," Davis said.</p><p>Seven million Americans have Alzheimer's, leaving families to navigate rising costs for <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/dementia-memory-care-cost-conservatorship-2026-8">memory care</a> facilities or home care. <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.alz.org/news/2025/november-national-family-caregivers-alzheimers-disease-awareness-month">One estimate</a> shows that lifetime costs for dementia can exceed $400,000.</p><p>Two dozen families <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/unprepared-for-dads-alzheimers-caregiving-lessons-learned-2026-8">navigating dementia</a> care told Business Insider that costs add up for frequent hospitalizations and physician visits, expensive medications, transportation costs, and round-the-clock home care. Those who can afford it spend five figures on monthly memory care facility costs. Other costs included home modifications, power-of-attorney legal fees, and technologies for <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tech-for-seniors-aging-at-home-care-bills-2026-7">aging in place</a>.</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Do you have thoughts to share about long-term care in the US? To share your story with a reporter, <strong>please fill out this </strong><a target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdg4AoiQ9q9GU2sU75z7cCrHvjt0JnM_0Nf34JYn_1DpF3w6A/viewform?usp=dialog"><strong>quick form</strong></a><strong>.</strong></p>
      </aside>
    <p>A report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that in 2025, one in four family caregivers cared for someone 50 and over with memory issues or dementia. While an estimated 7 million Americans aged 65 and over have Alzheimer's, that is expected to surge.</p><p>Wendy Rowland, 53, has cared for her husband with early onset Lewy body dementia for years. To manage his treatment, they spent through his 401(k) and sold their house of 20 years, then put him into a memory care facility two years ago that now costs $6,750 a month.</p><p>"I hope nothing like that happens with me, and if it does, I don't know if I would want anybody else to go through the same thing of having to figure out what to do," Rowland said.</p><h2 id="8aa301c6-67ad-4eea-95e6-10e3f662f8fd" data-toc-id="8aa301c6-67ad-4eea-95e6-10e3f662f8fd"><strong>The cost of memory care can be steep</strong></h2><p>It pained Keith Pavlick, 53, to witness his father slowly forget his family members' names and lose track of his surroundings. He hadn't fully anticipated the financial hit that came with it.</p><p>Pavlick, a real estate agent in Orlando, has helped his mother, 79, and his father, 80, since his <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/early-dementia-signs-missed-diagnosis-2026-7">dementia diagnosis</a> in March 2025. His parents moved into an assisted living facility for $9,000 a month.</p><p>The $9,000 is just the start, Pavlick told Business Insider earlier this year. He knows his dad will need a heightened level of care, and memory care facilities in his area cost $14,000 monthly.</p><p>"Unless you're starting out investing or bought SpaceX at the IPO, then you're probably not going to be able to take care of your parents when they're that age by yourself," Pavlick said. "I'm probably going to be selling real estate until I'm dead."</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad7cda16256d3825fdf969?format=jpeg" height="1152" width="1536" alt="Four people pose smiling at a restaurant table with drinks and diners in the background."><figcaption>Keith Pavlick helped his parents move into an assisted living facility.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Keith Pavlick</p></figcaption></figure><p>Memory care costs a median of about $8,000 monthly, according to data from SeniorLiving.org. They're more expensive than standard assisted living centers because dementia patients require 24/7 supervision by specialized caregivers. They also have high security and maintenance costs.</p><p>Medicare generally doesn't fund long-term memory care. Medicaid chips in for eligible families, though many said they have paid out of pocket or used <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/eldercare-crisis-long-term-care-costs-families-2026-8">long-term care insurance</a>.</p><p>Sharon Winterton, 53, has juggled working a tech sales job, raising a 14-year-old daughter, and caring for her 90-year-old mother with vascular dementia. Winterton moved her mom into an <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/living-in-senior-housing-before-retirement-2026-8">independent living</a> facility as her memory declined.</p><p>Her mom had invested in long-term care insurance, which she's used to cover her $7,000 monthly assisted living costs. Winterton said they're fortunate to avoid the high out-of-pocket cost, though she's splurged on technologies that allow her to change TV channels and monitor her mom remotely.</p><p>"Thankfully, I don't have to worry a lot about her long-term care," Winterton said.</p><h2 id="6adfdf7f-316a-4832-9d96-37b425512989" data-toc-id="6adfdf7f-316a-4832-9d96-37b425512989"><strong>There are many costs beyond direct care itself</strong></h2><p>Jenn Verser, 45, hadn't anticipated moving into her childhood home in New Jersey to help care for her dad with Alzheimer's.</p><p>Verser is selling her home and planning to build a two-story, roughly 1,000-square-foot addition to her <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/aging-parents-tiny-homes-yard-elder-care-2026-8">parents' house</a>. She expects it will cost at least $600,000, which they're planning to cover with a home equity line of credit, her parents' investment accounts, and the sale of her home.</p><p>She said it's important to get started as quickly as possible, so that her dad can get familiar and comfortable with the addition as his Alzheimer's progresses and confusion increases. Her parents will be moving into the addition, which is "elder-friendly," with the goal of aging in place. Verser, her husband, and her child will move into the main area. </p><p>Though some families told Business Insider they avoided memory care in favor of <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/aging-at-home-family-caregiving-costs-2026-8">at-home care</a>, the costs are often comparable. Tatyana Zlotsky, CEO of A Place for Mom, a platform connecting senior care providers and families, said that with home care costing about $30 an hour, based on the platform's internal data, this can end up being over $250,000 a year for 24/7 care.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad7d9e16256d3825fdf970?format=jpeg" height="6192" width="8256" alt="Michele Angela Brooks holding a pile of bills."><figcaption>Angela Davis said her mom&#39;s care has been pricey.<p class="copyright">Camille Farrah Lenain for BI</p></figcaption></figure><p>An <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/fire-financial-independece-early-retirement-investing-lifestyle-boredom-2026-3">early retirement</a> or remote job can help caregivers minimize costs. Families have invested thousands of dollars in age-tech designed for dementia care, such as motion-sensor cameras, medication monitoring, and smart home devices like stove shut-off devices. Others have spent five figures on home renovations for their loved ones.</p><p>Ann Gynn, 55, had cared for her mom until September, when she moved into memory care. In 2024, the content marketer in Cleveland started using JubileeTV, a remote caregiving platform allowing for remote monitoring through the TV, after many frustrating back-and-forth phone calls with her mom. Gynn created a schedule of her mom's favorite shows, and she sometimes uses the drop-in feature to see which nursing aides are in the room.</p><p>"It gives me peace of mind that I have ways to get in touch with her and ways to help her that I don't physically have to be there for," Gynn said.</p><h2 id="c50828b4-cea6-48a8-b2ff-d4af0f452ab0" data-toc-id="c50828b4-cea6-48a8-b2ff-d4af0f452ab0"><strong>Emotional costs can be a heavy burden too</strong></h2><p>For many families, the greatest cost of dementia care isn't financial.</p><p>For Michelle Keller, 59, caring for her dad has meant sacrificing going out for her 35th wedding anniversary, and, at times, forcing herself to feel optimistic. She said caregiving can be tiring and involve a lot of acting.</p><p>"To be able to put on that happy face, it helps to get things done," Keller said. "If they're happier, they'll listen and follow instructions a little better. There's a lot of work involved that honestly doesn't allow you to take time to think about the mess you're in."</p><p>Dementia caregivers said they've quit their jobs, gone part-time, or taken on less time-consuming roles to be more present as caregivers. The stress of worrying about falls, wandering, or medication takes a toll on caregivers' physical health, too. They don't always have the time or energy to prepare for their own long-term care.</p><p>"Asking individual people to find the Goldilocks solution of how much to save for a future even that may or may not occur is unfortunately the wrong question," said Alan Weil, senior vice president of public policy at AARP.</p><p>Laura Ehrlich, 54, knew her aunt's health was declining when, a few years back, she caught her giving her <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/laid-off-job-market-search-60s-social-security-bankruptcy-ageism-2026-9">Social Security</a> number to a scammer.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad7d2d6794a2984cfca926?format=jpeg" height="1287" width="1716" alt="Four people sit together on a couch in a warmly lit room with holiday decorations."><figcaption>Laura Ehrlich has cared for five loved ones over 20 years.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Laura Ehrlich</p></figcaption></figure><p>With help from an aide, she handled her day-to-day needs, but after her aunt fell at the mall, her family decided to place her in an assisted living facility nearby. Ehrlich, who also cares part-time for her mother-in-law, stays afloat by living on a stipend from her aunt's trust.</p><p>"I still haven't dealt with the loss of my parents, my husband, or my father-in-law," said Ehrlich, who has worked on and off in between caregiving. "It's just been putting up a wall and going on to the next person who needs help."</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/dementia-care-costs-memory-care-home-care-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>The CEO who leads one handwritten note at a time</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:42:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/twilio-ceo-khozema-shipchandler-handwrites-notes-leadership-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aac517816256d3825fdf299?format=jpeg" height="4592" width="6885" alt="A CEO in a zip-up jacket and collar shirt, smiling and holding a gavel at the Nasdaq during a celebration of his company's 10-year anniversary since its IPO."><figcaption>Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler in June at the Nasdaq, celebrating the company&#39;s 10th anniversary since its IPO<p class="copyright">NYSE: TWLO</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler writes notes to his company's 80+ leaders before their annual retreat.</li><li>He said the analog ritual is rooted in part in his own memories of being a junior employee at GE.</li><li>The notes also help him build relationships with those who could one day sit in Twilio's C-suite, he said.</li></ul><p>At least once a year, Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler's right hand cramps up from a few hours of writing. He's not signing copies of a book.</p><p>The pain, instead, comes from penning personalized notes to every member of the technology company's 80-plus-person leadership team ahead of their <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/boxing-helping-women-leaders-burnout-fight-co-lab-2026-1">annual retreat</a>.</p><p>"After every 10, I have to take a 30-minute break," Shipchandler told Business Insider of the deliberately analog ritual, which is rooted partly in his own memories of being a more junior employee at GE and how special it felt to have a senior leader take notice of him.</p><p>"I have no idea what the words were, I can't remember, but I definitely remember how I felt when that happened," said Shipchandler.</p><p>"If I can do that just for one person and it increases their confidence or their capacity or their desire to go do a hard thing, I think that's pretty awesome," he said.</p><p>Shipchandler, 52, added that the notes serve another purpose: helping him <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-leaders-can-build-emotional-intelligence-2021-2">build relationships</a> with people who could one day sit in Twilio's C-suite. He said they typically include a mention of a project or initiative the leader is driving; something complimentary about their leadership style; and encouragement for what's next.</p><p>"At some point I'm going to retire, and there's a new generation of people that I want to know intimately and that I want to know to know me intimately," Shipchandler said. "They are our bench."</p><h2 id="4ffe5579-6cdf-4db2-933d-32872ed6e5c3" data-toc-id="4ffe5579-6cdf-4db2-933d-32872ed6e5c3"><strong>'They're owed information'</strong></h2><p>Founded in 2008, Twilio provides technology that businesses use to interact with customers over phone calls, texts, and emails. Shipchandler <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/mckinsey-expanded-leadership-training-includes-navy-seals-2026-3">rose to the top job</a> at the company in 2024 — his first stint as CEO — after serving as president of communications and, before that, as operating chief and as finance chief. He spent 22 years at GE prior to joining Twilio in 2018.</p><p>Shipchandler's handwritten notes offer a window into his broader approach to leadership. He said he's committed to responding to employees' emails, texts, and Slack messages within 24 to 48 hours and that he makes a habit of reading meeting materials in advance to respect participants' time. He also said he aims to be a "straight shooter" rather than a CEO who papers over hard news with "corporate speak."</p><p>"My style is to be as transparent as I possibly can be," he said. "I do that because I think everyone — whether it's an employee or an investor or the board — they're owed information that they can make decisions about."</p><h2 id="2330edf6-98d5-4130-9162-fc9919530ffb" data-toc-id="2330edf6-98d5-4130-9162-fc9919530ffb"><strong>The next generation of leaders</strong></h2><p>Shipchandler oversees a roughly 5,500-person workforce with optional in-office attendance, a stance increasingly at odds with <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/companies-requiring-return-to-office-rto-mandate">policies at other large employers</a>, many of which have brought back white-collar workers at least part-time.</p><p>He said Twilio's remote-friendly model has held up on the metrics that matter to him: Productivity remained steady after the company went remote during the pandemic, while recruiting, engagement, and retention improved.</p><p>The arrangement has made it harder, though, to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/japan-workplace-culture-reshaped-my-expectations-of-work-2026-6">foster culture</a>.</p><p>"We recognize there are downsides," said Shipchandler, which is why he added that Twilio creates deliberate opportunities for employees to build relationships in person. These include periodic paid trips for team get-togethers and free lunch on Thursdays at the company's San Francisco headquarters.</p><p>Shipchandler has also taken a contrarian view of middle managers compared with some of<strong> </strong>Twilio's tech peers. Rather than trim their ranks and have those who remain rely more on AI, as companies including<strong> </strong><a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/meta-block-managers-player-coaches-org-leads-2026-4">Block and Meta</a> have done, he said that Twilio is continuing to invest in the midlevel cohort through training programs. Twilio's next generation of senior leaders could come from this group, he said, and managers bring something AI lacks.</p><p>"The thing that's hard to replace is judgment," said Shipchandler. "That's what the managers do."</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/twilio-ceo-khozema-shipchandler-handwrites-notes-leadership-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>A Lyft driver was in a crash on the job. Now he's struggling to provide — and fighting insurance.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:35:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/a-lyft-driver-crashed-on-the-job-now-hes-struggling-to-provide-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aada8d94a3706ac06f8505b?format=jpeg" height="1840" width="1208" alt="Osahon Aburime, a former Lyft driver, sits with sunglasses around his neck with a tan wall behind him, wearing a tan cap."><figcaption>Osahon Aburime, a former Lyft driver, was injured in a car accident.<p class="copyright">Osahon Aburime</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>A Lyft driver in North Carolina was involved in an accident while en route to pick up a passenger.</li><li>Sixteen months later, he's still fighting for an insurance payout.</li><li>He said that accident has also made it harder to support his family.</li></ul><p>Osahon Aburime opened his Lyft app on Mother's Day last year to make some money.</p><p>That day, the North Carolina driver had made about $80 to put toward taking his wife out to dinner and getting a gift for his mom. As he was on his way to pick up a passenger, though, he got into a car accident.</p><p>"All of a sudden, I just saw this car in front of me, so I stepped on my brakes," he said. "We just ran into each other."</p><p>Sixteen months later, he uses a cane to walk, he said. He tried unsuccessfully to return to work as a ride-hailing driver.</p><p>"I said, 'Let me see if I can continue to drive to make money for my family,'" he said. "But it just got to a point now I can't even bend down."</p><p>Aburime's experience shows one occupational hazard of working as a driver for a gig-work platform like Lyft or Uber. While the apps say they provide insurance coverage, the independent contractors doing the work often have fewer protections than traditional full-time employees.</p><p>"Safety is fundamental to Lyft and it is our goal to make every ride safe, comfortable and reliable," a Lyft spokesperson said. "We maintain auto liability insurance that meets local and state regulations."</p><h2 id="c0ea3789-7ac7-4a07-b09a-40fe18b0b506" data-toc-id="c0ea3789-7ac7-4a07-b09a-40fe18b0b506">'Nobody deserves this'</h2><p>After the accident, Aburime had pain in one of his feet, according to a report from the hospital viewed by Business Insider. He also lost the Chevy Malibu that he was driving when he got into the accident.</p><p>His income has also been affected. Before the accident, it was typical for him to make around $1,700 a month on Lyft. The money helped support his family, along with his wife's income working at an eye clinic.</p><p>Since the accident, though, he hasn't been able to earn money, he said. That led him to fall behind on payments toward his minivan, which his lender repossessed earlier this year, according to a notice seen by Business Insider.</p><p>Aburime has also been fighting to get a payout from Mobilitas, which provides ride-hailing insurance to Lyft. Aburime said that he's reached out to the North Carolina Department of Insurance for help. The department has told him to look for a lawyer — something he says he can't afford.</p><p>A day after the accident, Mobilitas denied Aburime's claim, according to the insurance documents he provided.</p><p>The denial contained incorrect information about the accident, though, including the wrong time, according to a letter sent from North Carolina's insurance department . It also suggested that Aburime wasn't on his way to pick up a passenger when the accident happened — something he denies.</p><p>The company has since corrected some of the details, but has continued to deny his claim. Mobilitas did not respond to a request for comment on this story.</p><p>Fighting for an insurance payout has taken time away from trying to find other work and recovering from his injuries, he said. "These rideshare companies tell you that you are covered if something like this happens," he said.</p><p>Other gig workers have faced their own challenges after suddenly not being able to work on apps like Uber and Instacart.</p><p>In some cases, the companies have <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-gig-workers-are-fighting-against-sudden-account-deactivations-2023-9">deactivated workers' accounts</a>, Business Insider previously reported. The company's policies say that workers can lose access to the apps by abusing them.</p><p>Some drivers have told Business Insider that they were kicked off the apps — and lost income — after an overcharge at a store checkout. One <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/instacart-shopper-won-280000-in-arbitration-after-deactivation-2023-9">Instacart worker</a> won $28,000 in back pay after a months-long arbitration process over such a deactivation.</p><p>Others, like Aburime, have tried to get <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/i-got-stabbed-while-working-for-instacart-2023-11">insurance settlements</a> after getting injured on a gig.</p><p>"I don't think any company should treat the people who work with them like this," Aburime said.</p><p><em>Do you have a story idea about Uber or Lyft? Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/a-lyft-driver-crashed-on-the-job-now-hes-struggling-to-provide-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I make up to $15,000 a month online answering appliance questions. I love the flexibility.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:30:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/technician-turned-justanswer-side-hustle-full-time-six-figure-job-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aabf69d4a3706ac06f84412?format=jpeg" height="1737" width="2316" alt="Matthew Morrison headshot."><figcaption>Matthew Rankin turned his side hustle online into his main job after burning out at his 9-to-5.<p class="copyright">Photo courtesy of Matthew Morrison</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Appliance technician Matthew Rankin quit his full-time job and went all in with his side hustle.</li><li>He now works nine to 10 hours a day answering questions online for JustAnswer.</li><li>The job can be hectic, but it is flexible and has allowed him to make up to $15,000 a month.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Matthew Rankin, a 52-year-old appliance technician based in Greenville, South Carolina. The following has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I wasn't happy with my work and was <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-avoid-burnout-hybrid-remote-work-switching-off-intensification-jobs-2025-5">getting burned out</a>. I've been an appliance expert for easily 25 years, specializing in dishwashers, refrigerators, and other appliances.</p><p>Maintenance in general is hard, but when you get into commercial properties and apartment maintenance, it's a whole other league. I worked in commercial property management for about six years, managing facilities and fixing whatever was broken. It wasn't the most glamorous job; you're always on call.</p><p>After doing that, I decided I would never be on call again.</p><h2 id="abf46b20-c669-4cda-b7b4-e1037806f3f5" data-toc-id="abf46b20-c669-4cda-b7b4-e1037806f3f5">I was looking for an opportunity to make more money on the side</h2><p>I was living in Charleston, South Carolina; it's an expensive region, and I didn't have much in savings. I think I saw a reel on Instagram <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/answering-questions-justanswer-expert-advice-rv-motorhome-online-2022-7">about JustAnswer</a>, and it looked too good to be true. I was hesitant at first, but I applied and figured I'd give it a couple of hours a day.</p><p>I'd log on to my computer and close out five or 10 calls or questions. I started seeing these part-time paychecks come in and saw the potential after doing the math, so I decided to go for it.</p><p>I was in a position that had a lot of flexibility. After about six months, I gave my <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-you-should-quit-job-right-future-employers-2025-9">two-week notice</a> and haven't looked back. Now I make between $10,000 and $15,000 a month answering questions online.</p><h2 id="b9fdd227-3e5b-4640-b387-fc8990016e21" data-toc-id="b9fdd227-3e5b-4640-b387-fc8990016e21">How I make money answering questions online</h2><p>When a question comes in, I can accept it or pass it, so it's important to filter them properly.</p><p>Sometimes the question is about a brand I've never heard of, or a product or situation I'm not familiar with. Questions from other countries pop up every once in a while, too. On JustAnswer, I may get a lot of refrigerator-not-cooling inquiries, and if it's a brand I know — LG, Kenmore, etc. — that's <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/justanswer-remote-side-hustle-work-from-home-boomer-expert-art-2025-2">a question I'll take</a>.</p><p>A lot of the people reaching out are DIYers, newer technicians in the field, or people who simply want access to someone with expertise. They're looking for guidance and help working through the troubleshooting process.</p><p>I gather as much information as I can quickly: the model number, whether I'll need to look up a part, and anything else I can quickly check on a second screen.</p><h2 id="309614ce-3b4e-4902-8e3e-be6d2e53e896" data-toc-id="309614ce-3b4e-4902-8e3e-be6d2e53e896">25 to 30 calls in a day is pretty good</h2><p>I can stay on text or be available for a phone call. I've made 50 calls in one day. It's not very common, but it's hectic. I've had phone calls up to an hour, although rare. As for text questions, they can take days, which isn't the goal and is also uncommon.</p><p>Sometimes the questions come in really fast, and I multitask with 10 windows open, five browsers, and the phone going at the same time. It takes a certain kind of person to be able to balance all of that.</p><p>The <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/flexible-side-gigs-parents-make-extra-cash-from-home-2020-9">hours are flexible</a>. I tend to stick to 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, but if I do something in the middle of the day, I might work a little later. Nine or 10 hours is probably average, but I'm not sitting in front of the computer working the entire time. If questions aren't coming in, I might play video games or play my guitar in the same room while I wait.</p><p>Some cons of working online and answering questions all day are that you need to be disciplined and treat it like <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/10-tips-work-from-home-stay-productive-and-happy-wfh-2021-9">a 9-to-5</a>, or you won't make the call load and will keep dropping pay rates. Some days, calls can be sparse; you never know. You hope for the best, make yourself available, and be ready.</p><h2 id="a8621d2e-8acd-44c6-9b48-c2cf70a59e97" data-toc-id="a8621d2e-8acd-44c6-9b48-c2cf70a59e97">I have no regrets about leaving my full-time job early — not a single one</h2><p>Something I wish I'd known sooner is to plan for your end-of-year taxes and set aside about 25% of each paycheck. Otherwise, I have no regrets.</p><p>My last job had no <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/interview-questions-about-career-opportunities-advancement-2022-3">opportunity for advancement</a> and would wear me down both physically and mentally. Advice I'd give someone looking to make a side hustle a full-time job: find something you are really good at and enjoy; the two will connect into something of value.</p><p>I fell into this incredible opportunity, and it's been life-changing. I've taken full advantage of it, and I do very well. It's not for everyone, but for people who value flexibility and want more balance, it can be a great fit.</p><p><em>Do you have an interesting side hustle to share with Business Insider? Email editor Manseen Logan at </em><a target="_blank" href="mailto:mlogan@businessinsider.com"><em>mlogan@businessinsider.com</em></a><em>.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/technician-turned-justanswer-side-hustle-full-time-six-figure-job-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>The Airbus A380 got a second life. Here's where you can still fly on the world's largest passenger jet.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:29:39Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/airbus-a380-routes-destinations-airlines-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9ab222a86b54c4431401d1?format=jpeg" height="2214" width="3547" alt="An Emirates Airline Airbus A380 airplane is directed on to a stand at Manchester airport in Manchester, U.K., on Thursday, Oct. 21, 2010"><figcaption>Emirates is the biggest operator of the world&#39;s largest passenger jet.<p class="copyright">Bloomberg/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Several airlines ditched the Airbus A380 during the pandemic.</li><li>But it's still flying high, led by Emirates' fleet of 117 superjumbos.</li><li>Business Insider compiled a list of every airline operating the A380 and their winter routes for 2026.</li></ul><p>Do you fancy flying on the <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/largest-passenger-planes-in-the-world-commercial-boeing-airbus-2022-6">world's largest passenger jet</a>?</p><p>The <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/british-airways-airbus-a380-premium-economy-review-upgrade-cost-2024-10">Airbus A380</a> has awed passengers for nearly 20 years. With a 262-foot wingspan, the superjumbo jet wouldn't fit on an NFL field.</p><p>Business Insider has compiled all the routes that it will fly this winter, based on Cirium data for November's schedule.</p><p>You can search for different cities in this table, then scroll down for more details about the airlines operating the A380.</p><div id="1788521180477" data-styles="default-width" data-embed-type="custom" data-script="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/MfcXN/embed.js" class="insider-raw-embed" data-type="embed"><div style="min-height:588px" id="datawrapper-vis-MfcXN"><script type="text/javascript" defer="" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/MfcXN/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-MfcXN"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/MfcXN/full.png" alt="A searchable table of every city that is served by the Airbus A380, and the destinations to which it connects." /></noscript></div></div><p>Airbus spent decades developing the double-decker airplane as an answer to the <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/50th-anniversary-boeing-747-queen-of-the-skies-passenger-flight-2020-1">Boeing 747</a>. It announced the project in 1990, but the A380 didn't enter service until 2007.</p><p>It has had a turbulent life ever since, falling in and out of popularity.</p><p>The European planemaker expected high demand for enormous aircraft due to the rise of airport megahubs like Dubai. It was ideal for Emirates, which operates the overwhelming majority of A380s.</p><p>However, many airlines preferred to fly point-to-point. Twin-jet aircraft like the Boeing 777 and Airbus A350 offer plenty of seats, greater flexibility, and lower operating costs.</p><p>The COVID-19 pandemic also prompted many airlines to rethink their strategies amid cost pressures. Air France and Malaysia Airlines were among those to retire all their A380s.</p><div id="1788521180477" data-styles="default-width" data-embed-type="custom" data-script="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3TqUv/embed.js" class="insider-raw-embed" data-type="embed"><div style="min-height:460px" id="datawrapper-vis-3TqUv"><script type="text/javascript" defer="" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3TqUv/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-3TqUv"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3TqUv/full.png" alt="A line chart showing the number of flights scheduled on Airbus A380s between November 2016 and November 2027, with separate lines for the total flights, and those operated by Emirates." /></noscript></div></div><p>Airbus built the last new A380 in 2021.</p><p>While COVID was a major blow, many airlines fell back in love with the superjumbo when lockdowns lifted.</p><p>Lufthansa retired all 14 of its A380s during the pandemic but has brought back eight of them since 2022. Etihad Airways reactivated six jets, too.</p><p>Meanwhile, Qantas restarted A380 flights between Sydney and Dallas/Fort Worth last August, for the first time since the pandemic. A year later, though, the Australian flag carrier said it was bringing forward its retirement of the planes to 2028.</p><p>Back in 2017, there were more than 10,000 flights a month operated by the A380. While that has since fallen to 7,500 for November, it seems there is still some life left in the superjumbo.</p><div id="slideshow"><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">1. Emirates</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9ab26aa86b54c4431401d4?format=jpeg" height="2087" width="2783" charset="" alt="An Emirates Airlines cabin crew attendant stands in the new bar area for the Airbus A380 aircraft during the unveiling at the ITB Travel Fair in Berlin, Germany, on Wednesday, March 8, 2017."><figcaption>Emirates&#39; A380s have a bar onboard.<p class="copyright">Bloomberg/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>Dubai's airline is by far the world's largest operator of the A380, with over nine times as many as any other operator.</p><p>Emirates has a total of 117, of which 85 are actively flying as of September, according to fleet data from ch-aviation. 13 are in storage, and 19 are undergoing maintenance.</p><p>Like its rival Middle Eastern airlines, Emirates' A380 is highly luxurious — with business-class passengers able to visit the bar or even book a shower.</p><p>The airline's president, Tim Clark, told Business Insider last year that he'd like&nbsp;Airbus to build a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/airbus-a380-makeover-resume-production-emirates-airline-tim-clark-2025-1">new version of the A380</a> with more fuel-efficient engines.</p><p>Emirates' plethora of planes comes with a similarly broad route map. Brace yourself for an extensive list.</p><p>Emirates flies the A380 between Dubai and Amman, Jordan; Amsterdam; Auckland, New Zealand; Bangkok; Barcelona; Bengaluru, India; Birmingham, England; Brisbane, Australia; Cairo; Casablanca, Morocco; Copenhagen, Denmark; Denpasar, Indonesia; Düsseldorf, Germany; Frankfurt, Germany; Glasgow, Scotland; Guangzhou, China; Hong Kong; Houston; Istanbul; Jeddah, Saudi Arabia; Johannesburg; Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; London; Los Angeles; Madrid; Manchester, England; Mauritius; Melbourne, Australia; Milan; Moscow; Mumbai, India; Munich; New Delhi; New York; Nice, France; Osaka, Japan; Paris; Perth, Australia; Prague; Rome; San Francisco; São Paulo; Seoul; Shanghai; Singapore; Sydney; Taipei; Tokyo; Toronto; Vienna; Washington, DC; and Zurich.</p><p>Emirates also operates three <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/flying-on-fifth-freedom-routing-from-new-york-to-singapore-2023-1">fifth-freedom flights</a> with the A380, between Christchurch, New Zealand, and Sydney; Bangkok and Hong Kong; and Milan and New York.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">2. British Airways</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a9ab113a86b54c4431401c2?format=jpeg" height="3024" width="4032" charset="" alt="British Airways' new first class suite that it is planning to retrofit onto Airbus A380s"><figcaption>British Airways is retrofitting a new first-class suite for the A380.<p class="copyright">Pete Syme/Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p><a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/british-airways-airbus-a380-premium-economy-review-upgrade-cost-2024-10">British Airways</a> has 12 Airbus A380s. According to ch-aviation, two of those are undergoing maintenance, and another is in storage, as of September.</p><p>As part of a $9 billion "transformation program," BA is retrofitting its A380s with an upgraded first class.</p><p>"The A380 is an important part of our fleet and rightfully, incredibly popular with our customers," Neil Chernoff, BA's chief planning and strategy officer, previously told Business Insider.</p><p>BA flies the A380 between London Heathrow and Johannesburg, Miami, San Francisco, and Singapore</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">3. Singapore Airlines</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6800db9a3fe8d39283634e9d?format=jpeg" height="5504" width="8256" charset="" alt="A view of the first class seating area during a media tour onboard a Singapore Airlines Airbus A380 at Singapore Changi Airport in Singapore on October 24, 2020."><figcaption>A first-class suite on a Singapore Airlines A380.<p class="copyright">ROSLAN RAHMAN/AFP via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/singapore-airlines-first-class-suite-double-bed-is-worlds-best-2024-6">Singapore Airlines</a> also has a fleet of 12 double-decker jets, having retired seven due to the pandemic.</p><p>The carrier is one of just 10 to receive a five-star rating from Skytrax. It named Singapore Airlines' business class the second-best, behind Qatar Airways, but the best for first class.</p><p>The airline offers enormous suites on its A380s, each with an armchair and a bed. Two of these can also be uniquely combined to create a double bed.</p><p>Singapore flies the A380 between Singapore Changi Airport and Auckland, London, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Delhi, Shanghai, and Sydney.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">4. Qatar Airways</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6696812b5439fb59cebdba44?format=jpeg" height="3333" width="5000" charset="" alt="Qatar Airways Airbus A380 aircraft as seen on final approach"><figcaption>A Qatar Airways Airbus A380.<p class="copyright">Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p><a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/qatar-airways-airbus-a380-not-retiring-boeing-777x-replacement-2024">Qatar Airways</a> cleaned up at last year's Skytrax awards, winning both best airline and best business class.</p><p>Like Emirates, the airline's A380 includes a bar for business-class passengers. It also has huge bathrooms, but lacks showers.</p><p>Qatar's A380s, perhaps surprisingly, don't feature its flagship business-class product, the QSuite, which you'll find on the A350, Boeing 777, and 787.</p><p>Following <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/boeing-777x-jet-cabin-what-passengers-can-expect-2026-9">delays to the Boeing 777X</a>, Qatar reversed plans to retire the A380.</p><p>Its former CEO, Akbar Al-Bakar, said in 2021 that buying the planes was a "big mistake," given their high operating costs.</p><p>However, on the sidelines of 2024's Farnborough Airshow, his successor Badr Mohammed Al-Meer — who has since left the CEO position — said the quad-engine was getting a new lease of life.</p><p>Qatar has eight A380s, which it operates between Doha and Bangkok, London, and Paris.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">5. Qantas</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/65dc7e1090413ab8e1d6b9a9?format=jpeg" height="3712" width="5568" charset="" alt="A Qantas Airways Airbus A380 takes off from Dresden Airport."><figcaption>A Qantas Airbus A380.<p class="copyright">Sebastian Kahnert/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p><a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/qantas-first-business-class-worlds-longest-flights-project-sunrise-pictures-2023-2">Australian flag carrier Qantas</a> has 10 A380s.</p><p>It flies them from Sydney to Dallas/Fort Worth, Johannesburg, Los Angeles, and Singapore — from which it also continues to London.</p><p>Plus, the A380 is sometimes used on flights from Melbourne to Los Angeles.</p><p>A severe storm warning and "incredibly high" demand during Taylor Swift's Australian tour last year saw Qantas use a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/taylor-swift-airline-replaced-three-flights-a380-qantas-sydney-melbourne-2024-2">spare A380 to fly Swifties</a> from Melbourne to Sydney.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">6. Etihad</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/669681a49caa6ed01e01f918?format=jpeg" height="2178" width="3000" charset="" alt="a general view of The Residence bedroom is seen on board a Etihad Airways Airbus A380."><figcaption>The Residence&#39;s bedroom on board an Etihad A380.<p class="copyright">Etihad Airways via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/etihad-airways-first-class-apartment-family-travel-points-worth-it-2024-5">Abu Dhabi's Etihad&nbsp;Airways</a> is the third-most prominent operator in the Middle East, often overshadowed by Emirates and Qatar.</p><p>However, its A380s are unique in offering the most extravagant ticket in commercial aviation: <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/etihads-a380-returning-to-nyc-see-residence-first-class-suite-2023-12">The Residence</a>.</p><p>For $24,000, you can book the only three-room suite on an airliner, complete with a bedroom and shower.</p><p>Etihad has 9 A380s, but one is in storage, according to ch-aviation.</p><p>It flies them from Abu Dhabi to Bangkok, London, Singapore, and Toronto.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">7. Lufthansa</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6800dc363fe8d39283634ea6?format=jpeg" height="5149" width="8129" charset="" alt="A Lufthansa Airbus A380 aircraft taxis to the hangar after landing at the airport in Munich"><figcaption>A Lufthansa Airbus A380 taxiing in Munich.<p class="copyright">Peter Kneffel/picture alliance via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>The German flag carrier has a fleet of eight A380s.</p><p>It appears to prefer the only other double-decker jet, as Lufthansa operates the most Boeing 747 jets of any passenger airline.</p><p>Lufthansa initially retired all 14 of its A380s during the pandemic before changing its mind as travel demand bounced back. The other six were sold back to Airbus, Airways Magazine reported in 2023.</p><p>Lufthansa's A380s go between Munich and Bangkok, Los Angeles, New Delhi, San Francisco, and Washington, DC.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">8. Korean Air</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/66851a24268f62ba18a708df?format=jpeg" height="2000" width="3000" charset="" alt="A Korean Air plane on the tarmac."><figcaption>A Korean Air Airbus A380.<p class="copyright">Matej Divizna/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p><a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/flew-korean-air-boeing-747-business-felt-like-private-jet-2023-9">Korean Air</a> is one of four airlines on this list, and 11 around the world, to be rated five stars by Skytrax.</p><p>It has five A380s, according to ch-aviation. It flies them on only one route: between Seoul's Incheon Airport and New York's JFK.</p><p>Back in 2021, CEO Walter Cho told&nbsp;FlightGlobal&nbsp;that its A380s would be retired by 2026, but delivery delays and high travel demand have seen their lifespan extended.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">9. Asiana Airlines</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/67ffe8d63fe8d39283633cdf?format=jpeg" height="2874" width="4089" charset="" alt="An Asiana Airlines Airbus A380 landing in Barcelona, Spain, in September 2024."><figcaption>An Asiana Airlines Airbus A380.<p class="copyright">Joan Valls/Urbanandsport /NurPhoto via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>Asiana Airlines has six A380s, one of which is in storage and another undergoing maintenance as of September, per ch-aviation's fleet data.</p><p>During the pandemic, <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/airbus-a380-ghost-planes-asiana-pilots-2020-7">Asiana flew empty superjumbos</a> to keep its pilots certified.</p><p>The second Seoul-based carrier on this list, Asiana, has merged with Korean Air. For now, it's operated as a subsidiary but will use the same name from 2027.</p><p>Until then, Asiana regularly flies these jets from Seoul to Bangkok, Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Sydney.</p></div></div><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">10. ANA</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6696834b5439fb59cebdbc2e?format=jpeg" height="1489" width="2500" charset="" alt="A ceremony to celebrate first delivery of Japan's All Nippon Airways (ANA) Airbus A380 aircraft, called the &quot;Flying HONU&quot;, is held after its arrival at Narita International airport on March 21, 2019"><figcaption>A ceremony celebrated the delivery of ANA&#39;s first A380 in 2019.<p class="copyright">JIJI PRESS/AFP via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p>ANA is the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/see-inside-ana-mammoth-airbus-a380-aircraft-all-nippon-airways-2023-4">newest Airbus A380 customer</a>, as its first was delivered in 2019.</p><p>The Japanese airline has three in total, which it flies between Tokyo's Narita Airport and Honolulu.</p><p>ANA is another five-star airline, with an impressive business-class product. But you'll need to fly on a Boeing 777 to experience "The Room" — or in first class, "The Suite," which includes a 43-inch TV.</p></div></div></div><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/airbus-a380-routes-destinations-airlines-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I raised my daughter to value making a difference over making money. Now I question that lesson.</title>
    <updated>2026-09-20T09:24:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/taught-child-prioritize-purpose-making-difference-life-lesson-might-regret-2026-9</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6aad8b234a3706ac06f84f29?format=jpeg" height="3780" width="4725" alt="The author (right) and her daughter pose in front of greenery."><figcaption>The author (right) and her daughter both founded nonprofits.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Miriam Bonilla.</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>My daughter and I both run nonprofits: mine rescues dogs; hers supports women's education.</li><li>We are both passionate about our philanthropic work, but it comes at a price.</li><li>I sometimes wonder if I should have encouraged her to choose a paycheck over passion and purpose.</li></ul><p>Two years ago, my daughter, Jordan, was in the outskirts of Marrakech in Morocco with a group of 15 Amazigh girls from the High <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/wealthy-pay-to-get-lost-wilderness-luxury-travel-2025-2">Atlas Mountains</a>. Displaced after a recent earthquake, they were in a temporary dorm, just a small house, but it was all they had available to them. My daughter was leading a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/after-losing-job-boyfriend-started-my-own-business-yoga-instructor">yoga teacher</a> training program through her nonprofit — one that she built herself from the ground up when she was 26.</p><p>"How hot is it?" I ask while sitting at my desk in Los Angeles, frantically putting together a fundraising plea for the charity I founded for a matted poodle mix with a broken leg. He was hit by a car, and one of our rescue volunteers just saved him and rushed him to our vets.</p><p>"44 Celsius, Mom, and no fans. Cell phone cutting out," she shares.</p><p>I quickly Google the Fahrenheit conversion and learn that it's about 111 degrees.</p><p>"Oh no!" I gasp.</p><p>"Texting you Hamza's number. Nice guy. He'll help," she says.</p><p>"On it!" I yell, but she's gone.</p><p>This is the path my daughter and I have chosen. We are both <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/day-in-the-life-claudia-romo-edelman-founder-sotol-romo-2026-5">founders of our own nonprofits</a>. Our roller coaster lives are filled with daily problem-solving and never-ending stress. I'm proud of the person my daughter has become, but now I sometimes wonder if I should have pushed her in a different direction.</p><h2 id="76fa0a1e-1d40-4eb8-a5dc-dc1c264dcc76" data-toc-id="76fa0a1e-1d40-4eb8-a5dc-dc1c264dcc76"><strong>I'm always ready to help</strong></h2><p>It was a cool 69 degrees where I was in Santa Monica, yet my whole body suddenly felt blazing hot. As mothers, we are always split in two, immersed in our own lives, but also wherever our children are, even if it's on the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/what-its-like-living-far-from-my-mom-abroad-2026-1">other side of the world</a>.</p><p>Within an hour of connecting with my daughter, I reached Hamza in Marrakesh, arranged for six large fans to be delivered C.O.D. by morning, and am laser-focused on raising $4,200 needed for the emergency pup who's already in surgery.</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>Do you have a parenting regret? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at <a target="_blank" href="mailto:jgoldblatt@insider.com">jgoldblatt@insider.com</a> to share your experience with Business Insider.</p>
      </aside>
    <p>That night, as I feed my current <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/kids-want-pet-parent-doesnt-adopts-dogs-unexpected-benefits-2026-4">pack of rescue dogs</a>, I ask myself the push-pull, ever-pervasive question: Should I have encouraged my daughter to choose something more stable and secure, but less noble?</p><p>I was raised in apartheid South Africa. My parents left with their three daughters, without trying to change a system they hated. As a young adult in America, I suffered from terrible guilt. Why did we just walk away?</p><h2 id="30d783f7-12fd-4286-9265-f4a0b6f13d81" data-toc-id="30d783f7-12fd-4286-9265-f4a0b6f13d81"><strong>I wanted to model something different for my daughter</strong></h2><p>"Make a difference. Leave a footprint on the planet. Care about others," was the mantra I later instilled in my only child as a single mother.</p><p>At the age of 9, Jordan, already passionate about causes, went off to protest to save spider monkeys, picketing with a sign.</p><p>When she was a teenager, I started rescuing dogs. Having always been a huge animal lover, all it took was saving one little Chihuahua to open my eyes to the plight of animals in need. My daughter saw how dramatically my life changed. Heels were replaced by flip-flops, hair appointments were sacrificed for vet visits, and gradually, mutts took the place of men. By the time she left for college, I had started my own dog rescue foundation.</p><h2 id="833f0aba-f20f-4174-ab33-d724d6f890d9" data-toc-id="833f0aba-f20f-4174-ab33-d724d6f890d9"><strong>My daughter often puts others first</strong></h2><p>My examples seemed to stick with her. During her sophomore year, Jordan studied abroad in Cambodia and volunteered at a school teaching English. It lit a fire that was already smoldering in her.</p><p>At 26, she founded Souljourn Yoga Foundation, raising funds for young women's education globally through ethical yoga retreats and partnering with NGOs on the ground.</p><p>Now, over a decade later, I've witnessed the joys but also the struggles she's experienced, many of which mirror my own.</p><p>How do we get more donors? Will that <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/grant-proposals-for-small-business-how-to-get-started-2011-11">grant proposal</a> be approved? Can we make it through the fiscal year? I lie awake at night and angst for us both.</p><h2 id="321ad7d9-dd04-419a-8add-70041dd9468f" data-toc-id="321ad7d9-dd04-419a-8add-70041dd9468f"><strong>I have mixed feelings now</strong></h2><p>People often say to us, "Thank goodness for angels like you!" But they don't see the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/quit-career-caregiving-healthcare-costs-social-security-working-grandchildren-2026-1">personal sacrifices</a> behind those words. There's the three major back surgeries I've had from lifting large dogs and heavy bags of food, and the five hours of sleep Jordan and I both average a night, consumed by our missions that neither of us can switch off, holding up our own heavens like Atlas, as it were.</p><p>But there are also nights when I lie in bed and cherish the magic moments. The 23 hours of air travel I took to hear the infectious, gleeful laughter of schoolchildren in Hikkaduwa, Sri Lanka, as they stretched their arms high in a yoga posture they had never done before. The glow I felt watching my daughter lead them, encouraging them to reach for the sky.</p><p>And recently, I received a text from the adopter of that injured poodle-mix we named Romeo. He's now a healthy, fluffy, racing-around pup who is loved and adored.</p><p>These are the riches that cannot be counted in dollars or measured by a bank balance.</p><p>Yet, with rising costs, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/nonprofit-director-stressed-about-federal-funding-how-to-cope-2025-2">declining funding</a>, and the future of many small nonprofits uncertain, I grapple daily with the question as her mother: Should I have encouraged my daughter to choose a paycheck over passion and purpose? These days, I'm not so sure I know the answer.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/taught-child-prioritize-purpose-making-difference-life-lesson-might-regret-2026-9">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-09-20T09:24:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">I modeled a life of service for my daughter. I'm proud of her, but I worry about the financial and personal costs we both face.</summary>
